name: Jonathan ben Uzziel is traditionally credited with an Aramaic Targum to the Prophets
note: Hillel’s leading disciple Jonathan ben Uzziel is associated with an Aramaic translation of Nevi’im.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 132

name: Jewish delegation again protests Archelaus to the emperor
note: Jews appealed to Augustus against Archelaus’s brutality.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 132

name: Archelaus is deposed and exiled
note: Augustus removed Archelaus from power and sent him into exile.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 132

name: Judaea is annexed to direct Roman administration
note: After Archelaus’s removal, Judaea was placed under direct Roman administration through governors/procurators.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 132

name: Herod Antipas continues limited rule in the north
note: Herod Antipas, Archelaus’s brother, retained a tetrarchy in Galilee and Perea under Roman sovereignty.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 132

name: Lawlessness and plunder spread after Archelaus
note: A period of insecurity involving local gangs, former soldiers and abusive officials.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 132

name: Sadducees establish a rival judicial council
note: The Tzedukim became politically active and maintained their own council or sanhedrin.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 132

name: Anti-Jewish disturbances unsettle Babylonian rural communities
note: A disturbance with anti-Jewish overtones connected with two private Jewish militia leaders in Babylonia.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 132

name: Rural Jews in Babylonia relocate toward larger cities
note: Rural Jews in Babylonia relocate toward larger cities.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 132

name: Agrippa I receives a limited Herodian realm
note: Agrippa I was released after an imperial succession and sent to rule part of the Herodian territories, later enlarging his authority.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Agrippa I becomes highly popular with many Jewish subjects
note: Agrippa I’s acceptance among the Tannaim and his popularity with the population.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Roman and Herodian authorities repeatedly replace High Priests
note: The high-priesthood as increasingly politicized and sometimes sold or reassigned frequently by rulers and governors.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Former High Priests develop violent patronage and militia networks
note: Repeated manipulation of the high-priesthood is associated with strong-arm factions that contributed to growing disorder in Judaea.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Sanhedrin leaves its former location in the Temple complex
note: The Sanhedrin withdrew from its respected place in the Temple amid escalating lawlessness and bloodshed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Sanhedrin relocation curtails capital jurisdiction
note: After the move the court no longer exercised the same status and could not impose the death penalty.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Rabbi Tzadok begins prolonged fasting for Jerusalem
note: Rabbi Tzadok perceived impending national catastrophe and began a long period of fasting that continued until the destruction era.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Jesus is executed by Roman authority according to Christian tradition
note: The execution of Jesus as a wider event in the Jewish-Roman setting, describing his criticism of powerful priestly groups and Roman execution on a treason charge.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Caligula orders imperial cult images including a statue for the Jerusalem Temple
note: Emperor Caligula demanded divine honors and ordered his image placed in temples; the Jerusalem Temple crisis threatened direct confrontation with Judaean Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Jews organize mass nonviolent opposition to the Caligula statue order
note: Jewish communities protested that installation of the imperial image in the Temple was religiously impossible.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Petronius delays implementation of Caligula’s Temple order
note: The Roman governor of Syria recognized that enforcing the statue decree could cause enormous bloodshed and delayed implementation while appealing to the emperor.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Philo leads an Alexandrian Jewish embassy to Rome
note: Philo of Alexandria made representations at Rome amid the broader crisis facing Jews under Caligula.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Caligula dies before the Temple statue order is carried out
note: Caligula’s death in 41 CE ended the immediate threat that his statue would be installed in the Jerusalem Temple.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Agrippa II enters the Herodian political system in Codex’s chronology
note: Agrippa II enters the Herodian political system in the traditional chronology.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Agrippa II aligns closely with Roman authorities
note: Agrippa II as increasingly dependent on Roman political power and connected to influential priestly groups.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Rabban Gamliel I dies
note: The death of Rabban Gamliel I, grandson of Hillel.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel I succeeds as Nasi
note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel I succeeded his father in the Sanhedrin leadership.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai serves as Av Bet Din
note: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai is placed in the senior judicial leadership alongside Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel I.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Queen Helena and the Adiabene royal family embrace Judaism
note: The conversion of Helena and King Monobaz from the region of Adiabene and their connection to Jerusalem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Helena and Monobaz support Jerusalem during famine
note: The Adiabene royal converts provided food relief and gifts during shortages in Jerusalem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Samaritans attack Jewish festival pilgrims
note: Samaritan attacks on Jews traveling to Jerusalem for pilgrimage festivals.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Sadducean judicial activity continues alongside rabbinic leadership
note: The Tzeduki council remained politically active during this period.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Political fragmentation deepens across Judaea
note: Widening factional division between accommodationists, elite power groups and increasingly militant anti-Roman nationalists.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 133

name: Radical anti-Roman nationalism becomes an organized political force
note: Groups seeking to expel Rome became increasingly influential as confidence in moderate political solutions declined.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Caesarea synagogue dispute helps trigger open revolt
note: Harassment around a synagogue in Caesarea and the Roman procurator’s handling of the dispute became one of the immediate triggers of wider Jewish rebellion.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Jewish factions revolt against the Roman procurator
note: Jewish factions revolt against the Roman procurator.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Agrippa II and the procurator are forced to leave Jerusalem
note: Agrippa II and the procurator are forced to leave Jerusalem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Priestly radicals reject a sacrifice associated with Roman authority
note: Priestly radicals reject a sacrifice associated with Roman authority.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Roman and Agrippan forces march on Jerusalem
note: Roman forces and troops loyal to Agrippa II attempted to reassert control over Jerusalem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Roman forces withdraw after defeat near Jerusalem
note: The first major Roman attempt to suppress the revolt failed, strengthening militant confidence.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Jewish rebels proclaim Jerusalem free from Roman rule
note: Following the Roman withdrawal, militant leaders asserted an independent Jewish polity in Jerusalem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Factional conflict intensifies inside Jerusalem
note: Even as the revolt expanded, political and military groups in Jerusalem increasingly fought one another over strategy and authority.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Nero appoints Vespasian and Titus to suppress the revolt
note: Emperor Nero sent Vespasian, accompanied by his son Titus, to restore Roman control in Judaea.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Intercommunal killings spread during the opening of the revolt
note: Jews being killed by local non-Jewish populations as imperial order broke down.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Vespasian arrives in Judaea to reconquer the province
note: Vespasian began the systematic Roman campaign against the Jewish revolt, first concentrating on the north.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Josephus commands Jewish forces in Galilee
note: Yosef ben Mattityahu—later the historian Josephus—held a major military command in Galilee during the opening Roman campaign.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 134

name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel I opposes Josephus’s Galilean position
note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel I unsuccessfully sought Josephus’s removal from command because of distrust of his political alliances.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Josephus surrenders to the Romans
note: Josephus surrendered during the Roman northern campaign and subsequently attached himself to the Roman command.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Josephus accompanies the Roman army and later records the war
note: After surrendering, Josephus traveled with the Romans and later wrote detailed accounts of the revolt and destruction.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Roman forces subdue much of the countryside around Jerusalem
note: As Vespasian’s campaign advanced, much of the surrounding country fell under Roman control, increasing pressure on Jerusalem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Jerusalem descends into violent factional civil war
note: Rival Jewish factions fought one another inside the city even while the Roman threat increased.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Jerusalem food stores are destroyed during factional fighting
note: Militia groups burned large food reserves, worsening the famine during the coming siege.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Militant factions impose an internal siege on Jerusalem
note: Militant factions impose an internal siege on Jerusalem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Rebel factions mint their own coins and claim independent authority
note: Several factions issued coinage and asserted rival claims to Jewish independence.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Passover pilgrims become trapped inside besieged Jerusalem
note: Large numbers of Jews who had come for Passover were unable to leave as the internal and external sieges tightened.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel I dies during the Jerusalem crisis
note: The Nasi died during the siege and suggests he may have been deliberately killed amid the civil conflict.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai escapes besieged Jerusalem
note: According to rabbinic tradition, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai escaped the city’s internal blockade in order to negotiate with the Roman command.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai secures continuation of Torah study at Yavneh
note: The foundational Yavneh tradition says he obtained Roman permission for a rabbinic academy that would preserve organized Jewish learning after Jerusalem’s fall.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Rabban Gamliel II is designated for the restored rabbinic leadership
note: The Yavneh arrangement is associated with Rabban Gamliel II’s future presidency.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Vespasian leaves the Judaean campaign after Nero’s death
note: As the Roman imperial succession crisis unfolded, Vespasian eventually left the direct siege campaign and returned toward Rome.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Titus takes command of the siege of Jerusalem
note: Titus assumed command of the final Roman siege, with hunger and disease becoming severe inside the overcrowded city.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Jewish factions unite against the final Roman assault
note: As Roman forces closed in, the rival Jewish factions were compelled to cooperate in the city’s defense.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Roman forces breach Jerusalem’s defenses
note: The breach of Jerusalem’s walls is dated to 17 Tammuz in its 69 CE chronology.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Second Temple is destroyed by Roman forces
note: Second Temple is destroyed by Roman forces.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Roman forces seize Temple vessels and carry them toward Rome
note: Sacred Temple vessels being taken by the Romans; the Roman triumph later famously displayed Temple spoils.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Catastrophic famine, disease and battle deaths accompany Jerusalem’s fall
note: More than one million Jewish deaths from battle, hunger and disease during the destruction crisis.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Codex marks the end of the Second Temple era
note: The end of the Second Temple era.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 135

name: Large numbers of Jewish captives are taken to Rome after the revolt
note: Almost 100,000 Jews were taken to Rome, with some forced into arena spectacles.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Jewish fortresses continue resistance after Jerusalem's destruction
note: Some strongholds continued resisting Roman forces after Jerusalem and the Temple had fallen.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Yavneh academy continues under Rabban Gamliel II
note: The post-Temple Sanhedrin-Academy continued at Yavneh under Rabban Gamliel II as Nasi; Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai attended periodically.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananyah travels to Rome to seek release of Jewish captives
note: Rabbi Yehoshua traveling to Rome to negotiate for Jewish prisoners.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Josephus writes his history in Rome under Flavian patronage
note: Josephus composed his historical works in Rome in contact with the Flavian court and Agrippa II.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Herodian ruling circles fade as separate Jewish institutions
note: The former high-priestly and Herodian elite, including Agrippa II's line, disappearing through assimilation into Roman society.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Roman control is restored over most of Judaea outside Masada
note: Rome controlled the rest of Judaea while Masada still resisted.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Vespasian orders confiscation of property left by Jews killed in the war
note: Property left by Jews killed in the war was ordered transferred to the emperor, creating inheritance disputes for survivors.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Masada falls to Roman forces
note: The last major fortress of the First Jewish-Roman War fell after a Roman siege.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai dies
note: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai dies.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananyah becomes Av Bet Din
note: Rabbi Yehoshua succeeded to the senior judicial role in the Yavneh leadership.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus is recognized as Chacham of the academy
note: Rabbi Eliezer special recognition as the academy's supreme scholar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Yavneh sages begin regular sessions to consolidate Torah law
note: Rabban Gamliel II, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer held sessions to resolve inherited disputes and consolidate post-Temple halakhah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Temple measurements and Yom Kippur service traditions are preserved in Mishnaic teaching
note: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is associated with Temple measurements and Rabbi Shimon Ish HaMitzpeh with the Yom Kippur service order.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Codex attributes Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer to Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus
note: Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer is attributed to Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 141

name: Roman governor attempts to seize Rabban Gamliel II
note: The Roman governor attempted to capture and kill Rabban Gamliel II.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Codex dates Roman plowing of Jerusalem and the Temple site to this year
note: Roman plowing of Jerusalem and the Temple site is dated to this year.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Shimon HaPakuli standardizes the eighteen core blessings of the Amidah
note: Shimon HaPakuli standardizes the eighteen core blessings of the Amidah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Shmuel HaKatan composes the blessing against informers or sectarians
note: Shmuel HaKatan composes the blessing against informers or sectarians.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Rabban Gamliel II, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer travel to Rome
note: The leading sages traveled to Rome seeking relief from Roman pressure on Jewish life.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Domitian succeeds Titus during the Jewish delegation's stay in Rome
note: Titus died and Domitian succeeded him while the sages were in Rome.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Codex records suspension of a planned anti-Jewish imperial decree
note: A Roman political ally sacrificing his life to secure suspension of a decree aimed at the Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Yavneh leadership reduces public Sanhedrin sessions after return from Rome
note: The sages kept a lower profile and handled major matters in a smaller leadership circle.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Onkelos is traditionally associated with an Aramaic Torah translation
note: Onkelos, described as a convert and disciple of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer, is credited with an Aramaic Torah translation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Rabbi Eliezer is excluded from the Yavneh scholarly circle
note: After refusing to withdraw unilateral rulings, Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus was placed under severe exclusion by the sages.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Leadership of Yavneh narrows to Rabban Gamliel II and Rabbi Yehoshua
note: With Rabbi Eliezer excluded, tension between Rabban Gamliel II and Rabbi Yehoshua became prominent.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Rabban Gamliel II is removed as Nasi after conflict with Rabbi Yehoshua
note: Following repeated public confrontations with Rabbi Yehoshua, the scholars temporarily removed Rabban Gamliel II.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 142

name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah is appointed Nasi
note: A large assembly appointed the young Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah to replace Rabban Gamliel II.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: The Yavneh assembly remembered as 'that day' resolves many disputes
note: The unusually full gathering decided numerous halakhic questions and is remembered in rabbinic literature as 'that day.'
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Rabban Gamliel II is reinstated and shares leadership with Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
note: Rabban Gamliel was later restored, with leadership shared in some form with Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Roman pressure forces the academy from Yavneh to Usha
note: The scholarly leadership left Yavneh for Usha in the Galilee.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Rabban Gamliel II's court moves from Usha to Tiberias
note: Continuing pressure forced another move from Usha to Tiberias and then elsewhere.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Four leading sages travel to Rome under Nerva
note: Rabban Gamliel II, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah and Rabbi Akiva traveled to Rome seeking relief.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Codex reports possible removal of a heavy Jewish tax under Nerva
note: Some sources credit Nerva with removing a heavy tax burden from Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Sanhedrin-Academy returns to Yavneh
note: After the Roman mission, the sages returned the academy from Galilee to Yavneh.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Trajan succeeds Nerva
note: Trajan succeeds Nerva.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Yavneh academy is abandoned again under persecution
note: The central academy was again abandoned because of Roman pressure.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Leading sages settle privately in Lod
note: The displaced sages gathered in Lod and held fasts and prayers during persecution.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Rabbi Akiva travels to Babylonia for calendar-related rabbinic work
note: Persecution required Rabbi Akiva to travel to Babylonia in connection with determination of the Jewish calendar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Rabban Gamliel II dies in Lod
note: Rabban Gamliel II died while the rabbinic leadership was based in Lod.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah continues as Nasi in Lod
note: After Rabban Gamliel II's death, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah continued in the presidential role.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Lod academy briefly regenerates under Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
note: A limited revival with as many as thirty-two scholars attending.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Persecution drives the sages from Lod back to Galilee
note: Renewed Roman pressure forced the rabbinic leadership to leave Lod for Galilee.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Sages hide in Tzippori
note: Even in Galilee, the sages could not operate openly and hid at Tzippori.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Jewish-Roman conflict devastates Alexandria and Egyptian Jewry
note: Catastrophic violence destroying most of Alexandria's ancient Jewish community during Trajan's reign.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Jewish communities in Cyrene and Cyprus enter the wider Diaspora Revolt
note: Armed Jewish resistance in Cyrene and Cyprus during the conflict.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 143

name: Hadrian succeeds Trajan
note: Hadrian became emperor and initially pursued a less expansionist policy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Codex says Hadrian initially permits rebuilding of the Temple
note: An initial permission to rebuild the Temple.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Hadrian orders punishment of perpetrators of anti-Jewish violence in Egypt
note: Surviving Jews of Egypt appealed successfully for punishment of those responsible for earlier massacres.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Some Jewish prisoners are released under Hadrian
note: Releases of Jewish prisoners early in Hadrian's reign.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Hadrian withdraws permission for Temple rebuilding
note: Hadrian reversed the earlier policy and withdrew permission to rebuild the Temple.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah dies
note: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah died after serving as one of the leading post-Yavneh sages.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Sanhedrin-Academy is re-established at Usha
note: The sages emerged from hiding and re-established their academy at Usha.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Rabbi Yehoshua leads at Usha as Av Bet Din
note: The elderly Rabbi Yehoshua served as Av Bet Din at Usha.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Shimon ben Gamliel II emerges as dynastic patriarchal leader
note: Shimon ben Gamliel II was recognized as heir to the Nasi dynasty, initially without full public exercise of the office.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Rabbi Yehoshua dies
note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananyah died, ending the career of one of the leading Yavneh sages.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Rabbi Akiva succeeds as Av Bet Din
note: Rabbi Akiva succeeded Rabbi Yehoshua in central rabbinic leadership.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Tradition records the death of thousands of Rabbi Akiva's disciples
note: Tradition records the death of thousands of Rabbi Akiva's disciples.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Hadrianic decrees restrict major Jewish religious practices
note: Bans affecting Shabbat, circumcision, and ritual immersion.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Hadrian plans Jerusalem as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina
note: Plans to rebuild Jerusalem as a pagan Roman city with a cult of Jupiter.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Codex reports deportations of Jews from Judaea to North Africa
note: Hadrianic policy included deportation of some Jews to North Africa.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Underground observance develops in response to Roman decrees
note: Underground observance develops in response to Roman decrees.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Armed resistance to Hadrianic rule begins to develop
note: Local armed resistance and guerrilla attacks emerging from underground opposition.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Regular Sanhedrin-Academy meetings cease during the crisis
note: The central rabbinic academy stopped regular meetings amid Roman repression and growing revolt.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Bar Kokhba revolt expands under Shimon bar Kosiba
note: Shimon bar Kosiba leading an increasingly organized and successful revolt against Rome.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Bar Kokhba forces use underground hideouts and guerrilla warfare
note: Prepared tunnels and underground systems used for surprise attacks.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Bar Kokhba's administration mints coins for a Jewish polity
note: The rebel administration issued its own coinage expressing Jewish political independence.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Codex says Bar Kokhba captures Jerusalem and declares it a free city
note: The revolt as taking Jerusalem and establishing a free Jewish city there.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Rabbi Akiva identifies Bar Kokhba as a potential Messiah
note: Rabbi Akiva identifies Bar Kokhba as a potential Messiah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Roman forces intensify the reconquest of Bar Kokhba territory
note: Rome gradually retaking outlying positions and fortified towns.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 144

name: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Shimon ben HaSgan are killed
note: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Shimon ben HaSgan are killed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Roman forces retake Jerusalem in Codex's reconstruction
note: Roman forces retook Jerusalem and pushed Bar Kokhba's remaining army toward Betar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Betar falls and the Bar Kokhba revolt ends in Codex's chronology
note: After a prolonged siege, Betar fell, Bar Kokhba was killed, and the revolt was crushed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Ancient tradition reports enormous Jewish casualties in the revolt
note: The figure of 580,000 Jews killed in battle and says many more died from starvation and later massacres.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Romans forbid burial of the dead after Betar
note: A Roman ban preventing Jewish burial of those killed after the revolt.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Large numbers of Jews are sold into slavery after the revolt
note: Extensive enslavement after Roman victory.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Jews are barred from Jerusalem after the revolt
note: Jews being expelled or excluded from Jerusalem after Roman victory.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Roman authorities impose a broad ban on Jewish religious practice
note: A decree of shmad prohibiting Jewish observance.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Rabbi Akiva is imprisoned
note: Rabbi Akiva's imprisonment is dated to 5 Tishrei during the Roman religious persecution.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Rabbi Akiva is executed by the Romans
note: Rabbinic tradition describes Rabbi Akiva being tortured and executed for continuing Torah teaching under Roman decrees.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Rabbi Yishmael and other Tannaim are remembered among the Ten Martyrs
note: Rabbi Yishmael and other Tannaim are remembered among the Ten Martyrs.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Younger disciples of Rabbi Akiva flee to Babylonia
note: Many younger Tannaim escaped Roman persecution and settled in Babylonia; Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira was associated with Nisibis.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Jews emerging from hiding suffer renewed Roman violence
note: Jews emerging from hiding suffer renewed Roman violence.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Tannaim begin returning from Babylonia
note: Some sages who fled the Hadrianic persecutions returned from Babylonia.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Small rabbinic gatherings resume without a full Sanhedrin
note: Returning sages met in smaller gatherings while avoiding immediate restoration of the formal central academy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Sanhedrin-Academy cautiously reconvenes at Usha
note: The Tannaim resumed organized sessions at Usha to reconstruct and clarify the post-Yavneh legal tradition.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Babylonian Tannaim migrate to Eretz Yisrael under Rabbi Natan
note: A group of Babylonian sages settled in Eretz Yisrael, led by Rabbi Natan, son of the Exilarch.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Rabbi Natan becomes a major figure in the restored academy
note: Rabbi Natan emerged as a leading Babylonian-born sage in the renewed Galilean academy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 145

name: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai travels to Rome to seek repeal of anti-Jewish decrees
note: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai was sent to Antoninus Pius and succeeded in having bans on Jewish observances lifted.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Permission is granted to bury those left unburied after Betar
note: Permission on 15 Av to bury the dead left from the Bar Kokhba catastrophe.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Sages institute the HaTov VeHaMetiv blessing in Birkat HaMazon
note: Burial permission is associated with institution of an additional blessing in Grace After Meals.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Sanhedrin-Academy moves to Shepharam
note: The central academy was established cautiously at Shepharam near Usha.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Rabbi Natan becomes Av Bet Din at Shepharam
note: Rabbi Natan as Av Bet Din is placed in the reconstituted academy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Rabbi Meir becomes Chacham of the academy
note: Rabbi Meir becomes Chacham of the academy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel II becomes Nasi
note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel II assumed the patriarchal presidency, though security concerns may have limited his public activity.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Tannaim organize halakhic material into tractates
note: The academy continued clarifying law and organizing the body of tradition into masechtot, a major step toward the Mishnah's later form.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai praises Roman public works while Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai criticizes them
note: A private rabbinic discussion about Roman infrastructure was reported to the authorities.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Roman authorities elevate Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai to public leadership
note: Rabbi Yehuda was honored and became Rosh HaMedabrim, a leading public spokesman or chairman.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Rabbi Yossi ben Chalafta is restricted to Tzippori
note: Rabbi Yossi, who remained silent in the discussion, was placed under local restriction or house arrest.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai goes into hiding from Roman authorities
note: After being condemned for criticism of Rome, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai fled and hid with his son Rabbi Elazar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his son are traditionally said to hide in a cave for thirteen years
note: Rabbinic tradition says Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar remained hidden for thirteen years.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Codex identifies Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon with the paytan Eleazar Kalir
note: Rabbi Elazar wrote many piyyutim under the name Eleazar HaKalir.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Leading figures of the previous Sanhedrin generation have died
note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel II, Rabbi Natan, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai had all died.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Roman military movement through Eretz Yisrael brings renewed suppression
note: Roman legions moving through the region during conflict with Parthia again disrupted Jewish communal life.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Jewish appeals bring relief from renewed Roman oppression
note: Jewish appeals succeeded in having renewed oppressive measures lifted.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi becomes active Nasi
note: Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel II, assumed formal patriarchal leadership and became known as Rebbi.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Codex associates Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi with Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is associated with Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi intensifies consolidation of the Mishnah
note: Rebbi continued collecting, selecting, and organizing earlier Tannaitic legal traditions into the concise form that became the Mishnah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Babylonian scholars migrate to Eretz Yisrael and strengthen the academy
note: Movement of scholars from Babylonia into Eretz Yisrael during Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's leadership.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi completes the Mishnah in Codex's chronology
note: The Mishnah as completed around this time after Rebbi's consolidation of Tannaitic legal traditions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi dies in Codex's chronology
note: Rebbi's death is placed around the same period as completion of the Mishnah while acknowledging later chronologies.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 146

name: Rabban Gamliel III succeeds Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi as Nasi
note: Rabban Gamliel III succeeded his father as patriarchal leader.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 147

name: Rabbi Yehuda Nessia I succeeds Gamliel III after a short interval
note: Gamliel III died after a short period and was followed by Rabbi Yehuda Nessia I.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 147

name: Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Oshiya preserve additional Tannaitic teachings as baraitot
note: Colleagues and disciples of Rebbi continued preserving material outside the Mishnah, especially collections of baraitot.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 147

name: Bar Kappara transmits additional baraitot
note: Bar Kappara transmits additional baraitot.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 147

name: Sifra and Sifri traditions continue to be organized
note: Preservation of halakhic midrash collections Sifra and Sifri is associated with the generation around the Mishnah and its immediate aftermath.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 147

name: Tosefta preserves additional material alongside the Mishnah
note: Additional Tannaitic material was preserved in the Tosefta during the transition from the Tannaitic to Amoraic period.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 147

name: Rav leaves Eretz Yisrael and settles in Nehardea
note: Rav (Abba Arikha), an elderly disciple of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and native of Babylonia, returned from Eretz Yisrael and settled in Nehardea, then a principal center of Babylonian Jewry.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 153

name: Persecution and insecurity intensify for Jews in Eretz Yisrael
note: Increased attacks and persecution in Eretz Yisrael and connects this instability with the growing importance of the Babylonian centers.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 153

name: Sasanian dynasty replaces Parthian rule in Babylonia
note: The Sasanian takeover of the Persian Empire brought Babylonia under a more centralized Zoroastrian monarchy, changing the political environment in which the large Jewish community lived.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 153

name: Religious tension grows between Sasanian authorities and Babylonian Jews
note: The establishment of Sasanian religious policy is associated with conflict affecting the Jewish population of Babylonia.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 153

name: Rabbi Yehuda Nessia I dies
note: The death of Rabbi Yehuda Nessia I during the decline of the centralized patriarchal academy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 153

name: Rabban Gamliel IV becomes Nasi
note: Rabban Gamliel IV becomes Nasi.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 153

name: Rabbi Yehuda Nessia II succeeds Gamliel IV as Nasi
note: After Gamliel IV's short tenure, the young Yehuda Nessia II succeeded as Nasi.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 153

name: Rav establishes the Sura academy
note: After the death of R. Shila, Rav left Nehardea and established a Metivta at Sura, teaching Mishnah and helping make Sura a major center of Babylonian Torah learning.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 153

name: Shmuel establishes a formal academy at Nehardea
note: Shmuel developed Nehardea into the other great early Babylonian center alongside Rav's Sura.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 153

name: Rabbi Yochanan establishes a Metivta in Tiberias
note: Rabbi Yochanan founded an academy in Tiberias that became the central focus of Amoraic scholarship in Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 153

name: Rabbi Oshiya's Caesarea academy has ended and Tiberias rises in importance
note: After Rabbi Oshiya's death, his disciple Rabbi Yochanan's academy increasingly displaced Caesarea as the principal Palestinian center.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 153

name: Semiannual Yarchei Kalla assemblies become a defining feature of Babylonian academies
note: The formal academy system in which scholars gathered in Elul and Adar for major study assemblies known as Yarchei Kalla.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 153

name: Rav has died by this time
note: Rav has died by this time.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Shmuel becomes the leading Talmudic authority in Babylonia
note: With Rav's death, Shmuel, head of Nehardea, became the senior Babylonian Amoraic authority.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Persecution again affects Jews in Eretz Yisrael
note: Renewed persecution of the Jewish community while Rabbi Yochanan remained the leading authority there.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Shmuel dies in Nehardea
note: Shmuel died without an immediate successor as head of the leading Babylonian center.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Rabbi Yochanan becomes the senior Talmudic authority
note: Rabbi Yochanan becomes the senior Talmudic authority.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Rav Huna becomes head of the Sura academy
note: Rav Huna assumed leadership at Sura, and the central Babylonian Talmudic authority shifted from Nehardea to Sura.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Nehardea is destroyed by forces associated with Papa bar Nazer
note: Nehardea, long a principal Jewish center, was destroyed during regional warfare. Its scholarly primacy did not recover, and many scholars relocated.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Rav Yehuda bar Yechezkel establishes the Pumbedita academy
note: Rav Yehuda founded an academy at Pumbedita, which replaced Nehardea as one of the two great Babylonian centers alongside Sura.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Twelve thousand Jews are reported killed when Shapur I suppresses a revolt
note: 12,000 Jewish deaths in one Persian possession during suppression of a revolt by Shapur I.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Diocletian reorganizes imperial rule in the Roman East
note: A major division of Roman imperial administration is placed under Diocletian and notes that Eretz Yisrael lay within the eastern sphere.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Diocletian distinguishes Jewish wine from imperial sacramental wine rules
note: Diocletian exempting Jewish wine from a sacramental-wine requirement while Samaritans did not claim the same Jewish status.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Rabbi Yochanan dies in Tiberias
note: Rabbi Yochanan died at great age after decades of leadership. His teachings and those of his circle formed a major foundation of the Palestinian Talmud.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Rabbi Ami succeeds Rabbi Yochanan's academy leadership
note: Rabbi Ami succeeds Rabbi Yochanan's academy leadership.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Rav Huna becomes the leading Talmudic authority
note: Rav Huna at Sura is identified as the recognized leader of the Amoraic scholars after Rabbi Yochanan's death.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 154

name: Rav Huna dies and is buried in Eretz Yisrael
note: Rav Huna dies and is buried in Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rav Chisda succeeds as head of Sura
note: Rav Chisda became Rosh Metivta of Sura after Rav Huna.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rav Nachman re-establishes the Nehardea scholarly tradition at Mahoza
note: The 'Metivta of Nehardea' was re-established in Mahoza under Rav Nachman.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rav Yehuda at Pumbedita becomes the leading Talmudic authority
note: Rav Yehuda at Pumbedita becomes the leading Talmudic authority.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rav Yehuda bar Yechezkel dies
note: The founder and head of the Pumbedita academy died.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rabbah bar Nachmani becomes head of Pumbedita
note: Rabbah succeeded Rav Yehuda as Rosh Metivta after Rav Yosef initially stepped aside.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rav Chisda becomes the leading Babylonian Talmudic authority
note: Rav Chisda at Sura is identified as the principal Babylonian authority after Rav Yehuda's death.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rabbi Yehuda Nessia II dies and Gamliel V becomes Nasi
note: The patriarchal office passed from Yehuda Nessia II to his son Gamliel V.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Roman persecution forces Rabbi Ami's academy from Tiberias to Caesarea
note: Rabbi Ami relocated the academy from Tiberias to Caesarea because of Roman persecution.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rabbi Avahu becomes the senior scholar in Caesarea after Rabbi Ami
note: Rabbi Avahu is identified as the senior scholar in Caesarea after Rabbi Ami's death.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rav Chisda dies and Sura again lacks a direct successor
note: Rav Chisda's death left Sura without an immediate Rosh Metivta.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rabbah becomes the leading Talmudic authority at Pumbedita
note: Rabbah becomes the leading Talmudic authority at Pumbedita.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rabbi Yehuda Nessia III succeeds Gamliel V as Nasi
note: The patriarchal succession from Gamliel V to Yehuda Nessia III.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Constantine grants official imperial favor and recognition to Christianity
note: Constantine's recognition of Christianity as a major turning point for Jews living under Roman rule.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Constantine sponsors Christian holy sites in Eretz Yisrael
note: Imperial construction of churches at Christian holy sites in the land.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rabbah dies while hiding from government authorities
note: Rabbah died in seclusion after being denounced to the government and sought by the authorities.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rav Yosef succeeds Rabbah as head of Pumbedita
note: Rav Yosef became Rosh Metivta and the central Talmudic authority.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Persecution drives many Palestinian Amoraim to Babylonia
note: Worsening conditions caused many Amoraim of Eretz Yisrael to flee to Babylonia.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rav Yosef has died and Abaye is chosen to head Pumbedita
note: After Rav Yosef's death, Abaye was selected from several candidates to lead the academy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Council of Nicaea separates the dating of Easter from dependence on the Jewish calendar
note: The Council of Nicaea is associated with Christian efforts to distance Easter calculation from the Jewish date of Pesach.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Abaye has died by this time
note: Abaye's death before Rava's succession.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Rava succeeds Abaye and moves the central academy to Mahoza
note: Rava succeeded as Rosh Metivta and transferred the central academy from Pumbedita to Mahoza, where he lived.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Roman Jewish immigrants establish a synagogue in Mahoza
note: Jews originating from the Roman world settling in Mahoza and maintaining their own synagogue.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 155

name: Jewish revolt against Gallus erupts in Galilee
note: A Jewish revolt against the Roman eastern ruler Gallus broke out in Galilee, with Sepphoris as a major center and fighting extending to other Jewish towns.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Roman forces suppress the Gallus revolt and devastate Jewish centers
note: General Ursicinus suppressed the revolt, damaging several Jewish centers in Galilee and beyond.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Roman pressure disrupts the traditional monthly Jewish calendar system
note: The mid-fourth-century persecutions is associated with restrictions on the Sanhedrin's witness-based new-moon and intercalation system.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Many remaining Palestinian Amoraim migrate to Babylonia
note: Most of the Amoraim still active in Eretz Yisrael fled to Babylonia during the crisis.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Palestinian Talmud reaches a late stage of formation
note: Palestinian Talmud reaches a late stage of formation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Babylonian Talmudic traditions are already taking recognizable form
note: By this period the Babylonian Talmud had begun taking form through accumulated Amoraic explanations and the debates of Abaye and Rava.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Rava dies
note: Rava died after leading the academy and serving as one of the central figures of the Babylonian Talmud.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak succeeds at Pumbedita
note: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak succeeds at Pumbedita.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua establish an academy at Naresh
note: A new Amoraic study center was opened near Sura at Naresh.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Ameimar becomes a central scholar in revived Nehardea
note: Ameimar becomes a central scholar in revived Nehardea.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Rav Kahana becomes a central scholar at Pum Nahara
note: Pum Nahara as another active Amoraic study center under Rav Kahana.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Hillel II becomes Nasi
note: Hillel II succeeded Yehuda Nessia III as Nasi during a period when the traditional calendar system was increasingly difficult to maintain.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Tradition associates Hillel II with organizing a continuous calculated Jewish calendar
note: Hillel II's leadership is associated with establishment of the continuous calendar that removed the need for monthly eyewitness declarations.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Julian becomes Roman emperor and encourages Jewish restoration hopes
note: Emperor Julian rejected Christianity as the imperial religious program and encouraged Jews, including through letters, in hopes of restoring Jerusalem and rebuilding the Temple.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Codex places formal establishment of the continuous Jewish calendar under Hillel II
note: Hillel II convened scholars during Julian's reign and established the continuous calculated calendar still used in later Judaism.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Julian dies during his Persian campaign
note: Julian died during military operations against the Sasanian Empire, ending the short period of imperial religious policy favorable to Jewish restoration hopes.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Anti-Jewish violence follows Julian's death in Eretz Yisrael
note: Renewed Christian attacks on Jews after Julian's death.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Rav Pappa dies
note: Rav Pappa died after leading the Naresh academy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Rav Ashi becomes head at Mata Mehasya near Sura
note: Rav Ashi became Rosh Metivta near Sura and gradually restored a recognized central Babylonian Talmudic authority.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Rav Ashi becomes the leading Talmudic authority
note: Rav Ashi's academy as the central authority in Babylonia.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 156

name: Rav Ashi and Ravina begin the great organization of Babylonian Talmudic material
note: Rav Ashi and Ravina begin the great organization of Babylonian Talmudic material.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Babylonian Gemara develops primarily on four orders of the Mishnah
note: No continuous Babylonian Gemara was organized on most of Seder Zeraim and Taharot, although many topics from those orders are discussed elsewhere.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Jewish residents leave Corinth after Visigothic invasion
note: Jews leaving Corinth after the Visigoths invaded Greece.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Christian authorities expel Jews from Alexandria
note: Expulsion of Alexandria's Jews under Christian authority during the patriarchate of Cyril.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Violence destroys the Jewish community of Minorca
note: A coercive Christian campaign on Minorca destroyed the synagogue and led to violence against the Jewish community.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Five hundred forty Jews of Minorca are reported converted to Christianity
note: Bishop Severus reported converting 540 Jews after the anti-Jewish campaign on the island.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Ravina I dies
note: Ravina I, colleague of Rav Ashi and a major late Babylonian Amora, died.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Rav Ashi dies after decades of leadership at Mata Mehasya
note: Rav Ashi died after a long period in which his academy became the principal center of Babylonian Talmudic scholarship.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Traditional chronology associates Rav Ashi's death with a major stage in the compilation of the Babylonian Talmud
note: Rav Ashi presided over the complete compilation of the Gemara into final form before his death.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Mareimar succeeds Rav Ashi as head of the Sura academy
note: Mareimar became Rosh Metivta after Rav Ashi while some students remained at Mata Mehasya.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Late Amoraim continue adding limited material after Rav Ashi
note: Later Amoraim continued to add minor editorial material to the Gemara after Rav Ashi's death.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: The Hillelite Patriarchate comes to an end under Theodosius II
note: After Gamliel VI's death, Theodosius II prohibited further fundraising for the office of Nasi and the institution effectively ceased.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Mareimar dies
note: Mareimar died after heading the Sura academy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Rav Iddi bar Avin succeeds as head of Sura
note: Rav Iddi bar Avin became Rosh Metivta of Sura.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Rav Iddi bar Avin dies
note: The death of Rav Iddi bar Avin.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Rav Nachman III bar Huna succeeds as head of Sura
note: Rav Nachman bar Huna became Rosh Metivta of Sura.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Rav Nachman III bar Huna dies
note: The death of Rav Nachman III bar Huna.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Mar bar Rav Ashi succeeds as head of Sura
note: The elderly Mar (Tivyumi) bar Rav Ashi became Rosh Metivta at Sura/Mata Mehasya.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Yazdegerd II restricts public Jewish Sabbath observance in the Sasanian Empire
note: A royal decree prohibiting Jews from observing Shabbat. Encyclopaedia Iranica independently describes a persecution beginning in 455 that forbade public Sabbath observance.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Vandals sack Rome and carry imperial treasures to North Africa
note: The Vandal sack of Rome and a tradition that Temple vessels taken to Rome in antiquity were among treasures carried to Africa.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 157

name: Mar bar Rav Ashi dies
note: Mar bar Rav Ashi dies.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 158

name: Rabbah Tospha'a succeeds as head of Sura
note: Rabbah Tospha'a succeeded Mar bar Rav Ashi as Rosh Metivta.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 158

name: Sasanian authorities arrest Ameimar, Exilarch Huna and Mesharshiya
note: The arrest of three prominent Jewish leaders by order of King Peroz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 158

name: Mesharshiya and Exilarch Huna are executed
note: Mesharshiya and Huna bar Mar Zutra, the Exilarch, killed on 18 Tevet.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 158

name: Ameimar is executed
note: Ameimar killed in Adar after the arrests of the Jewish leadership.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 158

name: Rabbah Tospha'a has died by this time
note: Rabbah Tospha'a had died before Ravina II's appointment.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 158

name: Ravina II becomes head of Sura
note: Ravina II becomes head of Sura.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 158

name: Synagogues in the city of Babylon are closed under Sasanian persecution
note: The closure of all synagogues in the city it identifies as Babylon and increasing pressure on the Jewish community.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 158

name: Jewish children are handed over to Zoroastrian priests during persecution
note: Many Jewish children being given over to priests during late-Sasanian persecution.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 158

name: Persecution contributes to Jewish migration out of Babylonia
note: A tradition that persecution encouraged migration from Babylonia toward Arabia, Egypt, North Africa and southern Europe.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 158

name: Ravina II dies on 13 Kislev in Codex's chronology
note: Ravina II is identified as the last Amora who had participated in the post-Ashi tradition and dates his death to 13 Kislev 4235.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 158

name: Codex marks the Babylonian Talmud as complete at Ravina II's death
note: The Babylonian Talmud as complete at Ravina II's death.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 158

name: R. Yosef heads the academy of Pumbedita at the opening of the Savoraic era
note: R. Yosef as Rosh Metivta of Pumbedita is placed at the beginning of the Rabbanan Savurai period.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: First generation of Savoraim undertakes limited clarification of the Babylonian Talmud
note: The Savoraim as the generation immediately following the Amoraim and says they introduced only very limited editorial and halachic clarifications where needed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: R. Rechumai, R. Tachana, Mar Zutra and two sages named R. Achai are listed among the early Savoraim
note: R. Rechumai, R. Tachana, Mar Zutra and two sages named R. Achai are listed among the early Savoraim.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Tradition attributes finalization of parts of the Pesach Haggadah to the Savoraim
note: An opinion that the Haggadah of Pesach was finalized in the early Savoraic period.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Tradition attributes the first written recording of the Babylonian Talmud to early Savoraim
note: An opinion that the first Savoraic generation may have committed the Talmud to writing.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Persecution of Babylonian Jews changes after the death of Peroz I
note: The earlier persecutions lost intensity after the death of the Sasanian king Peroz, but that a new form of pressure arose under his successor through support for a compulsory religious movement.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: R. Yosef has died by this time
note: R. Yosef, head of Pumbedita in its Savoraic chronology, had died by 520.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: R. Simuna succeeds R. Yosef at Pumbedita
note: R. Simuna succeeds R. Yosef at Pumbedita.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: R. Eyna becomes head of the academy of Sura
note: R. Eyna becomes head of the academy of Sura.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Exilarch Huna bar Kahana and many members of his family die
note: The deaths of Exilarch Huna bar Kahana and many of his family following a severe political and family dispute involving his father-in-law R. Chinena.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Mar Zutra is born posthumously into the exilarchal family
note: A posthumous son of Huna survived and was later named Mar Zutra; he would become Exilarch as a teenager.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Jewish Himyarite king Yusuf Dhu Nuwas is defeated and killed
note: Yusuf, the Jewish ruler of the Himyarite kingdom in southern Arabia, being killed when Ethiopian forces conquered his kingdom.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Aksumite conquest ends the Jewish-ruled Himyarite kingdom
note: The Ethiopian/Aksumite conquest ended the rule of Yusuf Dhu Nuwas and the Jewish monarchy of Himyar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Justinian issues anti-Jewish restrictions affecting synagogues in Byzantine North Africa
note: Justinian ordered all synagogues closed. More precisely, Justinian's Novella 37 of 535 prohibited Jewish worship in newly reconquered North Africa and provided for synagogues there to be confiscated and converted to churches.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Forced conversion occurs under Justinian in at least one North African Jewish community
note: Forced conversion under Justinian. External Jewish historical references specifically document the community of Borion being forced to accept Christianity and its synagogue converted into a church.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Tradition links a ban on reciting the Shema with its insertion into Mussaf Kedusha
note: An opinion that a decree against public recitation of the Shema led Jews to insert the declaration into the Kedusha of Mussaf as camouflage.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Fifteen-year-old Mar Zutra becomes Exilarch
note: Fifteen-year-old Mar Zutra becomes Exilarch.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: R. Simuna has died by this time
note: R. Simuna had died by 540.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: R. Reva'i succeeds R. Simuna as head of Pumbedita
note: R. Reva'i succeeds R. Simuna as head of Pumbedita.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: R. Eyna has died and Sura is left without a successor
note: R. Eyna had died and that local persecution prevented appointment of a new Rosh Metivta at Sura.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Persecution disrupts the leadership of the Sura academy
note: The Sura academy's leadership remained vacant because of local persecution.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: R. Yitzchak, a leading Babylonian scholar, is killed during persecution
note: The killing of R. Yitzchak during a local persecution shortly before Mar Zutra's revolt.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Mar Zutra proclaims a measure of Jewish self-rule in Babylonia
note: Exilarch Mar Zutra rebelling against local Sasanian rulers and establishing a degree of Jewish independence around Mahoza.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Mar Zutra's forces begin armed resistance to Sasanian authority
note: Mar Zutra's forces begin armed resistance to Sasanian authority.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 163

name: Sasanian forces defeat Mar Zutra's Jewish self-rule
note: Persian forces overwhelmed Mar Zutra after seven years of Jewish self-government.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: Mar Zutra and R. Chinena are executed at Mahoza
note: Mar Zutra and his elderly grandfather R. Chinena being hanged at Mahoza near Ctesiphon after the revolt was defeated.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: Persecution of Babylonian Jews intensifies after Mar Zutra's defeat

source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: A son is born to Mar Zutra and is named Mar Zutra II in Codex
note: A son was born at the time of Mar Zutra's execution and was named Mar Zutra II.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: R. Reva'i has died by this time
note: The death of the long-lived R. Reva'i by 560.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: Persecution causes the Pumbedita academy to relocate toward Firuz-Shabur
note: Because of persecution, the Pumbedita Metivta was later transferred to Firuz-Shabur near Nehardea before eventually being reconstituted at Pumbedita.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: Final Savoraim make limited editorial adjustments to the Gemara
note: Final Savoraim make limited editorial adjustments to the Gemara.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: Savoraic editing is treated as the final permitted adjustment to the Talmudic text
note: After the final Savoraim no new additions, deletions or editorial changes were accepted, apart from later scribal variants and marginal glosses.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: Tradition attributes compilation of the Masechtot Ketanot to the Savoraim
note: An opinion that the Savoraim compiled smaller tractates such as Sofrim, Semachot and Kalla from earlier Tannaitic and Amoraic material.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: Jews of Clermont face baptism or expulsion
note: Bishop Avitus's campaign against the Jewish community culminated in an ultimatum: accept baptism or leave Clermont. More than 500 Jews were baptized and those who refused departed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: Jews who refuse baptism flee Clermont for other communities
note: Jews who rejected baptism left Clermont; Marseille is specifically identified in external Jewish historical sources as a place of refuge.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: King Chilperic I compels many Jews in the Frankish kingdom to accept baptism
note: Frankish king Chilperic I forcing many Jews to become Christians.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: Some Jews baptized under Chilperic continue to practice Judaism secretly
note: Many of those compelled to convert remained secretly Jewish.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: Pumbedita academy reconstituted; Geonic era begins
note: Pumbedita academy reconstituted; Geonic era begins.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: The Geonic academies develop an international responsa network
note: The Gaon as the official head of a Babylonian yeshiva and presents Bavel as the centre of Jewish life during the Geonic centuries. Questions in halacha arrived from many countries; the academies discussed them and issued concise responsa under the presiding Gaon, generally in Aramaic.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 164

name: Mar Zutra II moves from Bavel to Eretz Yisrael

source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 165

name: Sura academy reconstituted
note: The Metivta of Sura was reconstituted after its earlier interruption, and R. Mar bar R. Huna became its Gaon.

note: Visigothic Spain orders Jews to convert or leave.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 165

name: Persian conquest allows Jews to return to Jerusalem
note: Persian forces captured Eretz Yisrael, including Jerusalem, from Byzantium. Jews were then allowed to settle in Jerusalem after nearly five centuries of exclusion.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 165

name: R. Chana Gaon becomes Gaon of Pumbedita
note: R. Chana Gaon became Gaon of Pumbedita, succeeding R. Maari Surgo.

source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 165

name: Heraclius issues an unsuccessful forced-baptism decree
note: Emperor Heraclius later decreed that Jews throughout the Byzantine Empire should be subjected to forced baptism, though the decree was not successfully implemented.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 165

name: Jewish tribes of northern Arabia are massacred and expelled
note: Several of Muhammad’s campaigns in northern Arabia is associated with the massacre and expulsion of Jewish tribes that did not accept the new religion, and says later expulsions were carried out in the name of fulfilling his wishes.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 165

name: R. Yitzchak I becomes Gaon of Firuz-Shabur
note: R. Yitzchak I becomes Gaon of Firuz-Shabur.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 165

name: Arab conquests link the Jewish communities of the Islamic world
note: The Muslim Arab conquest of Bavel from Persia and of Eretz Yisrael from Byzantium, together with Syria, Egypt, North Africa and later Spain. Political unification made communication easier between these Jewish communities and the Babylonian academies.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 166

name: R. Huna I becomes Gaon of Sura
note: R. Huna I became Gaon of Sura, succeeding R. Chanina II.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 166

name: R. Sheshna (Mesharshiya bar Tachlifa) becomes Gaon of Sura
note: R. Sheshna (Mesharshiya bar Tachlifa) became Gaon of Sura, succeeding R. Huna I.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 166

name: Bustenai becomes the first Exilarch under Arab rule
note: Bustenai as the first Reish Galuta under the new Arab-Islamic rule in Bavel and records a later controversy over the status of children said to have been born to an unconverted Persian royal woman given to him by the caliph.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 166

name: R. Yitzchak Gaon and the Jews of Nehardea welcome Caliph Ali

name: Sura succession becomes entangled in Exilarchic politics
note: Sura succession becomes entangled in Exilarchic politics.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 166

name: A wooden mosque is built on the Temple Mount; Jewish property confiscated
note: The Muslim ruler of Jerusalem built a large wooden mosque on the site of the Beit Hamikdash and confiscated Jewish property in Eretz Yisrael for redistribution to Arab settlers.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 166

name: R. Chanina III becomes Gaon of Sura
note: R. Chanina III became Gaon of Sura. His appointment followed years of political manipulation by the Reish Galuta.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 166

name: R. Huna Mari (Huna II) becomes Gaon of Pumbedita

name: Visigothic authorities accuse Spanish Jews of plotting revolt
note: Visigothic authorities accuse Spanish Jews of plotting revolt.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 166

name: R. Nahilai becomes Gaon of Sura
note: R. Nahilai became Gaon of Sura, succeeding R. Chanina III.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 166

name: Muslim conquest of Spain transforms Jewish life
note: Jews welcomed the Muslim invaders of Spain; many secret Jews returned openly to Judaism, Jews assisted the new rulers, and Jewish communal life in Spain subsequently began to flourish.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 166

name: R. Yaakov HaKohen (Yaakov I) becomes Gaon of Sura
note: R. Yaakov HaKohen (Yaakov I) became Gaon of Sura, succeeding R. Nahilai.

note: Many Jews in the Byzantine Empire were forced to accept Christianity, and many left Constantinople and other parts of the empire.

source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 167

note: Khazar ruler and many subjects convert to Judaism.

note: R. Acha(i), author of She’iltot, was passed over for the Pumbedita Gaonate in favour of R. Natroy amid Exilarchic involvement. He left Bavel and settled in Eretz Yisrael.

note: R. Yehudai Gaon (Yehuda II) became Gaon of Sura, succeeding R. Acha I. He was brought to Sura by the Reish Galuta Shlomo bar Chisdai and became noted for lucid Talmudic clarifications.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 167

name: R. Acha I becomes Gaon of Sura
note: R. Acha I became Gaon of Sura, succeeding R. Mari Kohen I. He served for approximately half a year.

name: Anan ben David establishes the movement later associated with Karaism
note: Anan ben David founded a Jewish sect—possibly after being passed over for the Exilarchate—which later became known as, or merged with, the Karaite movement.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 168

note: R. Hilai I became Gaon of Sura, succeeding R. Bibi HaLevi.

note: R. Yeshayah HaLevi became Gaon of Pumbedita, succeeding R. Menasheh.

note: The caliph in Baghdad placed Jerusalem under the protection of Charlemagne, the Frankish ruler and newly proclaimed western emperor. It also records a tradition that Charlemagne settled some Talmud scholars in Germany and France.

note: Reish Galuta Ukva attempted to redirect money raised for the Sura academy to his own benefit. R. Kohen Tzedek I opposed him. Ukva was expelled from office and central Bavel, later restored by the caliph, and then expelled again after public protest.

note: A view that during the dispute with Exilarch Ukva, R. Amram was appointed by Ukva as Gaon of Sura during R. Natrunai II’s tenure, but exercised none of the position’s rights or powers.

note: Byzantine Emperor Basil I decreed forced conversion of the Jews of southern Italy. R. Shephatia ben Amittai of Oria travelled to Constantinople and, according to some accounts, succeeded in having the decree lifted for Oria and its surroundings.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 171

name: R. Tzemach considers traditions conveyed by Eldad HaDani
note: R. Tzemach I was asked to rule on the validity of singular halachic opinions conveyed by the traveller Eldad HaDani, who claimed descent from the lost tribe of Dan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 171

name: R. Amittai and R. Silano contribute to the Italian piyyut tradition
note: R. Amittai succeeded his father R. Shephatia as a community leader and wrote piyyutim, while R. Silano of Venosa also composed piyyutim. The entry places these families within the old Jewish communities of southern Italy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 171

name: R. Yaakov III becomes Gaon of Sura
note: R. Yaakov III became Gaon of Sura, succeeding R. Shalom.

name: Five-year dispute over the Pumbedita Gaonate begins
note: The scholars of Pumbedita appointed R. Mevasser as Gaon, while Reish Galuta David ben Zakkai sought to install R. Kohen Tzedek II. The dispute lasted five years; David eventually recognized R. Mevasser, though some scholars continued with R. Kohen Tzedek.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 171

name: Ben Meir calendar controversy divides Jewish communities
note: Aharon ben Meir, head of the academy in Eretz Yisrael, announced a Rosh Hashanah date that differed from the calculation of the Babylonian Geonim. R. Saadia, then associated with Egypt, argued forcefully for the Babylonian position. The dispute disrupted calendars in many communities for several years before the Babylonian calculation prevailed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 171

name: R. Yom Tov Kahana becomes Gaon of Sura
note: R. Yom Tov Kahana became Gaon of Sura, succeeding R. Yaakov III.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 174

name: Arab attack on Oria kills and enslaves Jews
note: Some Jews were killed and many were enslaved when Arab forces attacked Oria in southern Italy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 174

name: R. Kohen Tzedek II Kahana becomes Gaon of Pumbedita
note: R. Kohen Tzedek II Kahana became Gaon of Pumbedita, succeeding R. Mevasser.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 174

name: Sura nearly disbands after the death of R. Yom Tov Kahana
note: After R. Yom Tov Kahana died, the remaining scholars at Sura considered dissolving the academy and moving to Pumbedita. David ben Zakkai appointed R. Natan as Gaon, but he died before taking office, leaving the academy without an immediate suitable candidate.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 174

name: R. Saadia Gaon becomes Gaon of Sura
note: R. Saadia Gaon became Gaon of Sura. David ben Zakkai appointed the relatively young R. Saadia in an effort to revive the Sura academy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 174

name: Saadia Gaon and David ben Zakkai enter a major political dispute
note: R. Saadia refused to sign judicial documents favouring Reish Galuta David ben Zakkai. Each side appointed a rival to the other’s office; the dispute spread widely and required caliphal recognition. The caliph backed David, and Saadia withdrew from public life for a period while R. Yosef served nominally as Gaon of Sura.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 174
