note: An attack on Girona's Jews on 9 Elul.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: Perpignan Jewish community is attacked
note: Perpignan among the communities attacked in the 1391 wave.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: Mass forced conversion creates a greatly enlarged converso population
note: Large numbers of Jews converting publicly under threat while many continued Jewish practice secretly, producing the enlarged population known as Anusim, Conversos or Marranos.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: The Rivash flees Spain and becomes rabbi in Algiers
note: R. Yitzchak ben Sheshet (the Rivash) fled the Spanish massacres and went to Algiers, where he became rabbi.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: The Rashbatz flees Spain for Algiers
note: R. Shimon ben Tzemach Duran (the Rashbatz) fled the Spanish massacres and settled in Algiers.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: R. Ephraim AlNakava flees Spain for North Africa
note: After his father was killed, R. Ephraim ben Yisrael AlNakava fled Spain for North Africa.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: R. Chisdai Crescas works to rebuild Spanish Jewish communities
note: Despite losing his son, R. Chisdai Crescas remained in Spain and worked to rebuild devastated Jewish communities.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: R. Chisdai Crescas composes Or HaShem and anti-Christian polemical works around this period
note: Crescas is associated with Or HaShem and Bitul Ikarei HaNotzrim in the aftermath of the 1391 crisis.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: Profiat Duran composes anti-Christian polemical works
note: R. Yitzchak Profiat Duran wrote Kelimat HaGoyim and the satire Al Tehi KaAvotecha in response to Christian pressure.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: A Jew is burned alive in Damascus and others tortured after mosque-fire accusation
note: A Jew burned alive and other Jews tortured in Damascus after accusations of setting fire to a mosque.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: Nimukei Yosef is composed in Spain
note: R. Yosef Chaviva's Nimukei Yosef commentary on the Rif is placed in this period.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: Most Jews flee Baghdad during the Tatar conquest
note: Almost all Baghdad Jews fleeing when Tatar forces conquered the city.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: Venice requires all Jews to wear a yellow badge
note: A yellow-badge requirement for all Jews of Venice.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: Paris Jews are attacked on Yom Kippur and seven are imprisoned
note: An attack on Parisian Jews on Yom Kippur and the imprisonment of seven Jews on an accusation involving an apostate.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 205

name: Final medieval expulsion removes Jews from most of France
note: Shortly after the Paris incident, Jews were expelled from most of France, with limited exceptions in parts of Provence.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: All Jews are expelled from Basel
note: A complete expulsion of Basel's Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: Eighty Jews are killed in Prague after an apostate’s accusation
note: The killing of about eighty Jews in Prague after accusations that they had insulted Christianity.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: R. Yom Tov Lipmann Mühlhausen is imprisoned and escapes
note: R. Yom Tov Lipmann Mühlhausen is imprisoned and escapes.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: Tatar conquest brings massacres of Jews in Syria
note: Massacres of Jews in Syria during the Tatar conquest.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: Seventy-seven Jews are killed in Prague riots
note: Seventy-seven Jews killed in anti-Jewish riots in Prague in Elul.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: Schaffhausen blood libel leads to thirty Jews being burned
note: Thirty Jews burned at the stake in Schaffhausen after a blood-libel accusation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: Salzburg ritual-desecration accusation kills Jews and expels survivors
note: Salzburg ritual-desecration accusation kills Jews and expels survivors.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: Jews are expelled from Speyer
note: Jews are expelled from Speyer.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Corfu Jews are required to wear a distinctive badge
note: A special-badge requirement for Jews on Corfu.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: Kraków blood-libel riot brings torture, execution and forced conversion
note: A blood-libel riot in Kraków, including the public torture and burning of one Jew and forced conversion of others.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: Rashbatz becomes rabbi of Algiers after the Rivash
note: R. Shimon ben Tzemach Duran (the Rashbatz) became rabbi of Algiers after the Rivash's death.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: Rashbatz composes major responsa and Magen Avot
note: The Rashbatz is associated with his responsa collection Tashbatz and Magen Avot during his Algiers leadership.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: Anti-Jewish legislation in Castile sharply restricts Jewish life
note: Legislation promoted by the converted bishop of Burgos restricting Jewish economic life and imposing red badges, distinctive clothing and hair/beard rules.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: Disputation of Tortosa begins under coercive conditions
note: Jewish representatives, including R. Yosef Albo, were compelled to participate in the lengthy Disputation of Tortosa under Benedict XIII and Gerónimo de Santa Fé.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 206

name: Disputation of Tortosa concludes after prolonged missionary pressure
note: The disputation continued into 1414 and ended after sustained missionary pressure; subsequent restrictions targeted Jewish books and communities.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Tortosa aftermath brings forced conversions and censorship pressure on the Talmud
note: The disputation as resulting in forced conversions and an order removing passages defined as anti-Christian from the Talmud.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: All Jews are expelled from Koblenz
note: The expulsion of the Jewish community of Koblenz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: All Jews are expelled from Cochem
note: The expulsion of the Jewish community of Cochem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Jewish women in Salzburg are ordered to wear bells on their dresses
note: A humiliating dress regulation requiring Jewish women in Salzburg to wear bells.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Wiener Gezera begins with imprisonment and confiscation of Austrian Jews
note: In the opening phase of the Wiener Gezera, Austrian Jews were imprisoned and their property confiscated following a ritual-desecration accusation at Enns.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Wiener Gezera culminates in mass burning and expulsion
note: 212 Jews burned in 1421, widespread forced baptism, further executions in Styria and expulsion of most remaining Austrian Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: R. Aharon Blumlein of Neustadt is killed in the Wiener Gezera
note: R. Aharon Blumlein, a disciple of R. Shalom of Vienna and author in the laws of niddah, was killed in the Austrian persecutions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Fifty-eight Jews of Styria are burned
note: Fifty-eight Jewish victims burned in Styria during the Wiener Gezera period.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: R. Yisrael Isserlein flees after his mother is killed
note: The future author of Terumat HaDeshen fled Austria after his mother was killed in the Wiener Gezera.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Jews of Chomutov are massacred in Hussite-era violence
note: The massacre of Chomutov's Jews by Hussite forces.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Jews are expelled from Cheb for alleged support of the Hussites
note: An expulsion of Jews from Cheb amid accusations connected with the Hussite conflict.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Jews are expelled from Jihlava for alleged support of the Hussites
note: An expulsion of Jews from Jihlava amid accusations connected with the Hussite conflict.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Jews are readmitted to Speyer
note: Jews are readmitted to Speyer.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: All Jews are expelled from Cologne
note: The expulsion of the Cologne Jewish community.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Jews are expelled again from Jihlava
note: Another expulsion of the Jews of Jihlava.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: All Jews are expelled from Bern
note: The expulsion of all Jews from Bern on 13 Iyar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: The Maharil dies
note: R. Yaakov Moellin (the Maharil), a leading Ashkenazi authority whose customs became highly influential, died on 21 Elul.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: All Jews are expelled from Fribourg
note: The expulsion of Fribourg's Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Sicilian Jews are ordered to attend conversion sermons
note: A compulsory-sermon order imposed on Sicilian Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Blood-libel persecution at Constance kills Jews and expels survivors
note: Fifteen Jews burned across Constance, Lindau and Ravensburg in a blood-libel persecution, followed by expulsions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Blood-libel persecution at Lindau kills Jews and expels survivors
note: Fifteen Jews burned across Constance, Lindau and Ravensburg in a blood-libel persecution, followed by expulsions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Blood-libel persecution at Ravensburg kills Jews and expels survivors
note: Fifteen Jews burned across Constance, Lindau and Ravensburg in a blood-libel persecution, followed by expulsions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 207

name: Jews are expelled from Meissen

note: The expulsion of Schaffhausen's Jews.

note: The expulsion of Bamberg's Jews.

note: The expulsion of Jews from Sélestat.

note: 1481 as the beginning of active Spanish Inquisition proceedings focused heavily on Conversos suspected of secretly practicing Judaism.

note: The expulsion of Perugia's Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 210

name: All Jews are expelled from Gubbio
note: The expulsion of Jews from Gubbio in 1486.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 210

name: All Jews are expelled from Vicenza
note: The expulsion of Jews from Vicenza in 1486.

note: Sefer HaAgur is printed in Naples.

note: Another expulsion of the Salzburg Jewish community.

name: About two thousand Anusim are killed in Lisbon
note: About two thousand Anusim killed in Lisbon.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 218

name: A Jew is stoned to death in Venice after a blood libel
note: An angry crowd stoned a Jew to death in Venice following a blood-libel accusation.

name: R. Yitzchak Abarbanel dies in Venice
note: R. Yitzchak Abarbanel dies in Venice.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 218

name: Jews are expelled from Ljubljana
note: The expulsion of Jews from Laibach/Ljubljana.

name: Jews of Tlemcen are required to wear a yellow patch
note: Following the conquest, Jews in Tlemcen were required to wear a yellow patch on their headgear.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 219

name: Hebron’s Jews are attacked; many are killed or flee
note: An attack on the Jews of Hebron, with many deaths and a large flight from the community.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 219

name: Jews are expelled from Württemberg
note: A regional expulsion from Württemberg.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 219

name: Jews are expelled from Regensburg
note: The expulsion of the Regensburg Jewish community.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 219

name: Jerusalem’s Jews are blamed for a water shortage and heavily fined
note: During a severe water shortage, Jerusalem's Jews were blamed and compelled to pay heavy fines.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 219

name: R. Yosef Karo begins writing the Beit Yosef in Adrianople
note: After moving to Adrianople, R. Yosef Karo began the Beit Yosef, his comprehensive study of halachic development written as a commentary on the Tur.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: Jewish captives on Rhodes help the Ottomans conquer the island
note: 2,000–3,000 Jews who had been brought to Rhodes as slaves aided the Ottoman conquest; Rhodes subsequently developed into a vibrant Jewish centre.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: Jews leave Cranganore after the Portuguese conquest and resettle in Cochin
note: Most Jews left Cranganore after Portuguese conquest and moved to Cochin, where the local ruler granted protections.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: Cairo Jews escape a threatened massacre and institute Purim Mitzrayim
note: A local ruler threatened to massacre Cairo's Jews unless they paid an enormous tax. His death in a counter-rebellion on the payment day led the community to institute Purim Mitzrayim on 28 Adar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: R. Eliyahu Mizrachi dies in Constantinople
note: R. Eliyahu Mizrachi, a leading Ottoman rabbi and major supercommentator on Rashi, died in Constantinople.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: Carpentras Jews are ordered to wear yellow hats
note: Pope Clement VII ordered the Jews of Carpentras to wear yellow hats.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: R. Yosef Joselmann protects Alsatian Jews during the Peasants’ War
note: Through negotiations during the Peasants' War, R. Yosef Joselmann of Rosheim helped prevent attacks on the Jews of Alsace.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: Jews are expelled from Hungary during Ottoman invasion
note: A broad expulsion of Jews from Hungary as Ottoman armies invaded; many moved into Ottoman-ruled Balkan regions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: Anusim reach Mexico despite ancestry restrictions; some are executed
note: Anusim reach Mexico despite ancestry restrictions; some are executed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: Thirty Jews are burned at Pezinok after a blood libel
note: Thirty Jews were burned in Pezinok after a blood-libel accusation; the surviving Jews were expelled.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: R. Yosef Joselmann is forced into a public debate with an apostate
note: Joselmann was compelled to debate an apostate on Rosh Chodesh Av; the apostate was subsequently expelled from Augsburg.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: R. Yosef Joselmann persuades the emperor that Jews are not Ottoman spies
note: Joselmann successfully countering accusations that Jews were spying for the Ottoman Empire.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: German Jews are required to wear a yellow badge
note: A broad requirement that Jews in the German lands wear a yellow badge.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: Shlomo Molcho and David Reuveni are arrested at Regensburg
note: After promoting a messianic-political mission, Shlomo Molcho and David Reuveni travelled to Regensburg, where imperial authorities arrested them.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: Shlomo Molcho is burned at the stake for refusing conversion
note: Shlomo Molcho was burned in Kislev after refusing to convert to Christianity.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 220

name: Jews are expelled from Constance
note: The expulsion of Constance's Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: Jews are massacred and enslaved during the Spanish capture of Tlemcen
note: Jews are massacred and enslaved during the Spanish capture of Tlemcen.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: Jews are killed and enslaved when Tunis is sacked
note: Many Jews killed and many others captured and sold as slaves when Tunis was ransacked.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: R. Yosef Karo settles in Safed
note: Karo moved to Eretz Yisrael and settled in Safed, where he became part of an extraordinary concentration of rabbinic scholarship.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: A royal order breaks the Jewish boycott of Kraków’s converted printers
note: After the brothers who founded the first Jewish printing press in Poland converted to Christianity, Jews boycotted their books until a royal order broke the boycott.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: Jews are killed at Trnava in a blood libel
note: Jewish deaths at Trnava in another blood-libel episode.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: R. Yaakov Bei Rav attempts to restore classical semicha in Safed
note: Supported by major Safed scholars including R. Yosef Karo, R. Yaakov Bei Rav attempted to revive classical rabbinic ordination under the Rambam's legal model; R. Levi ibn Chaviv strongly opposed the effort.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: Jews are expelled from Trnava after the earlier blood libel
note: The Jewish community of Trnava was expelled following the accusations of the preceding years.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: Orchot Tzadikim appears in Yiddish
note: The appearance of an anonymous Yiddish version/work identified as Orchot Tzadikim.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: The Portuguese Inquisition begins active persecution of Anusim
note: The Portuguese Inquisition beginning active operations against Anusim, including executions in Lisbon.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: Jews are massacred in Bohemia after an expulsion order
note: A massacre of Jews in Bohemia following an order to expel them from the country.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: Jews are expelled again from Naples
note: Jews who had resettled in Naples were expelled again.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: R. Yosef Karo completes the Beit Yosef
note: Karo completed his Beit Yosef commentary on the Tur on 11 Elul, after roughly twenty years of work.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: R. Ovadya Seforno writes his commentary on the Torah
note: Seforno's Torah commentary is placed in this year.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 221

name: Kalisz Jews are attacked in anti-Jewish riots
note: Anti-Jewish riots directed at the Jews of Kalisz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Jews are expelled from Mühlhausen and other Saxon towns
note: Expulsions from Mühlhausen and other towns in Saxony is associated with the influence of Martin Luther's increasingly anti-Jewish writings.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Jews are permitted to return to Brandenburg after Joselmann’s intervention
note: R. Yosef Joselmann's representations is credited with helping secure Jewish readmission to Brandenburg.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Possible debate between R. Yosef Joselmann and John Calvin
note: Some identify Joselmann as the Jew who debated John Calvin in an episode recorded in Calvin's writings.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Salonika fire kills two hundred Jews and destroys thousands of houses
note: 200 Jewish deaths and destruction of 5,000 houses in a major Salonika fire.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Anti-Jewish riots in Treviso kill Jews and drive out survivors
note: Many Jews killed in Treviso riots, after which the remaining Jews left the town.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Jews are expelled from Genoa again
note: Another expulsion of Genoa's Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Tatar forces attack the Jews of Bratslav
note: Jews in Bratslav were attacked during a Tatar invasion.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Austrian Jews are required to wear a yellow badge
note: A yellow-badge requirement for Jews in Austria.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: The last Jews of Bavaria are expelled
note: This expulsion as removing the last remaining Jews from Bavaria.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Radvaz leaves Egypt and settles in Eretz Yisrael
note: The elderly Radvaz moved first to Jerusalem and then to Safed, where he continued writing responsa and commentary on the Rambam.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: R. Betzalel Ashkenazi succeeds Radvaz in Egyptian leadership
note: R. Betzalel Ashkenazi, later known for Shitta Mekubetzet, succeeded Radvaz as a leading Egyptian rabbinic authority.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: A convert to Judaism is burned alive in Rome
note: A former monk who had converted to Judaism being burned alive in Rome.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Pope Julius III orders suppression and burning of the Talmud
note: The papacy ordered the Talmud burned and its printing halted because of alleged anti-Christian material.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: The Inquisition stages a massive burning of Jewish books in Rome
note: On Rosh Hashanah, the Inquisition staged a mass burning of Talmudic and other Jewish books in Rome; similar burnings followed elsewhere in Italy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: More than a thousand Talmuds and hundreds of Rif volumes are burned in Venice
note: More than 1,000 Talmud volumes and 500 copies of the Rif burned in Venice.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Dona Gracia Mendes Nasi settles in Constantinople
note: Dona Gracia left Ferrara and settled in Constantinople, where she used her wealth and networks to support Jewish learning, refugees and Anusim.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Rome’s Jews are confined to a ghetto and subjected to dress and economic restrictions
note: Pope Paul IV ordered Jews in Rome and other cities into locked ghettos; Jewish men were required to wear yellow hats and women yellow kerchiefs, alongside severe economic restrictions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 222

name: Twenty-six Portuguese Anusim are burned in Ancona
note: Twenty-six Portuguese Anusim who had openly returned to Judaism were executed by papal order in Ancona.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: Three Jews are killed at Sochaczew in a ritual-desecration libel
note: Three Jews killed at Sochaczew after a ritual-desecration accusation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: Jews are expelled from major Bohemian cities
note: Jews who had returned after earlier expulsions were again expelled from major Bohemian cities, though some were allowed back shortly afterwards and a few remained in Prague.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: R. Mordechai Yaffe leaves Prague for Italy
note: R. Mordechai Yaffe, later known for the Levushim, left Prague during the expulsions and spent about a decade in Italy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: About 7,500 Jews die in a Marrakesh cholera epidemic
note: Roughly 7,500 Jews, many descended from Spanish and Portuguese exiles, died in a cholera epidemic in Marrakesh.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: Ten thousand Jewish books are burned in Cremona
note: The Inquisition ordered a massive burning of Jewish books in Cremona.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: The Zohar is printed in Cremona
note: Despite the book burnings, a recently established non-Jewish-owned press printed the Zohar in Cremona.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: A Yiddish Chumash is printed in Cremona
note: The Cremona press printed a Chumash with a Yiddish translation in the year following the Zohar edition.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: R. Yosef Karo completes the Shulchan Aruch
note: Karo completed the Shulchan Aruch on 17 Adar as a concise practical code based on the Beit Yosef. Its later pairing with the Rema's Ashkenazi glosses became central to halachic consolidation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: Jews are expelled from Nový Jičín
note: The expulsion of Jews from Neutitschein/Nový Jičín in Moravia.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: Jews of Polotsk are drowned for refusing forced baptism
note: Jews of Polotsk are drowned for refusing forced baptism.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: Maharam Padua dies
note: R. Meir Katzenellenbogen (Maharam Padua), a disciple of R. Yaakov Pollak and R. Yehuda Mintz, died on 10 Shevat.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: Lithuanian Jewish men and women are marked by yellow clothing
note: Jewish men were required to wear yellow hats and Jewish women yellow kerchiefs in Lithuania.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: Jews are expelled from the remaining Genoese province
note: Jews expelled from the rest of the Genoese province; later return was permitted.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 223

name: R. Yisrael Horowitz and R. Moshe ben Yoel are burned in Prague
note: R. Yisrael HaLevi Horowitz and his son-in-law R. Moshe ben Yoel were burned to death in Prague.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 224

name: Pius V expels Jews from most of the Papal States
note: Pius V expels Jews from most of the Papal States.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 224

name: Shulchan Aruch is published with the Rema’s Ashkenazi glosses
note: Publication of the Shulchan Aruch together with R. Moshe Isserles's Hagahot/Mapah integrated Ashkenazi rulings and customs into the code and helped make it a transregional halachic standard.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 224

name: The Inquisition formally establishes a tribunal in Peru
note: The establishment of an inquisitorial tribunal in Peru as the formal arrival of the Inquisition in South America.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 224

name: The Ari arrives in Safed
note: After years of study near Cairo, R. Yitzchak Luria (the Ari) settled in Safed and joined its kabbalistic scholarly circle.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 224

name: Ramak dies in Safed
note: R. Moshe Cordovero (Ramak), author of Pardes Rimmonim and a major systematizer of Kabbalah, died in Safed on 23 Tammuz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 224

name: Anti-Jewish riots begin in Berlin over accusations against Lippold
note: Anti-Jewish unrest began in Berlin after accusations against the court Jew and administrator Lippold.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 224

name: The Ari dies in Safed during an epidemic
note: R. Yitzchak Luria died in Safed on 5 Av at age 38 after a short but transformative period of teaching Kabbalah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 224

name: R. Chaim Vital begins preserving the Ari’s teachings
note: After the Ari's death, his principal disciple R. Chaim Vital preserved and organized the oral teachings in notes that became foundational to Lurianic Kabbalah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 224

name: Maharal moves from Moravia to Prague and opens the Klaus yeshiva
note: R. Yehuda Loew (Maharal) left his long-standing Moravian rabbinate and settled in Prague, where he opened a yeshiva known as the Klaus.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 224

name: Lippold is executed and Jews are expelled from Berlin and Brandenburg
note: Lippold was executed after refusing conversion, and the Jews were expelled from Berlin and the whole province of Brandenburg.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 224

name: The Rema dies in Kraków
note: R. Moshe Isserles (Rema), whose glosses integrated Ashkenazi practice into the Shulchan Aruch, died on Lag BaOmer.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 224

name: The Maharshal dies in Lublin
note: R. Shlomo Luria (Maharshal), author of Yam Shel Shlomo and Chochmat Shlomo, died in Lublin on 12 Kislev.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: R. Avraham di Boton encounters Karo’s Kesef Mishneh while writing Lechem Mishneh
note: While writing Lechem Mishneh on the Rambam, R. Avraham di Boton encountered Karo's similar Kesef Mishneh, an episode he dated to 5 Adar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: R. Eliyahu de Vidas completes Reishit Chochma in Safed
note: The Ramak's disciple R. Eliyahu de Vidas completed the mussar-kabbalistic work Reishit Chochma on 18 Adar II.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: R. Yosef Karo dies in Safed
note: R. Yosef Karo died in Safed on 13 Nisan shortly after further editions of the Shulchan Aruch and Kesef Mishneh appeared.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: R. Moshe Alshich writes Torat Moshe Alshich
note: R. Moshe Alshich's biblical commentary and homiletic work Torat Moshe Alshich is placed in this period.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: R. Shmuel Uceda writes Midrash Shmuel
note: R. Shmuel Uceda, a disciple of the Ari, wrote Midrash Shmuel on Pirkei Avot.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: R. Gedalyah ibn Yachya leaves Italy for Alexandria
note: The chronicler R. Gedalyah ibn Yachya left Italy and settled in Alexandria.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: Twenty Jews are killed in anti-Jewish riots in Poznań
note: Twenty Jewish deaths in anti-Jewish riots in Poznań.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: Jews of Rome and Ancona are forced to attend conversion sermons
note: Pope Gregory XIII ordered Jews in Rome and Ancona to attend Christian conversion sermons.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: The Council of Four Lands emerges as the central Jewish authority in Poland
note: Around 1580, the Va'ad Arba Aratzot developed into the central autonomous Jewish governing body of Crown Poland, coordinating taxation, welfare, legal decisions and communal policy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: Yosef Saralvo is burned in Rome after returning openly to Judaism
note: The Portuguese Anus Yosef Saralvo, arrested in Ferrara, was burned in Rome with other returnees to Judaism.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: Matanot Kehuna is completed in Poland
note: R. Yissachar Ber HaKohen completed Matanot Kehuna, his commentary on Midrash Rabbah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: R. Shmuel Yaffe writes Yefei To’ar in Constantinople
note: R. Shmuel Yaffe, rabbi of the Ashkenazi community is placed in Constantinople, at work on Yefei To'ar on Midrash Rabbah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: R. Pinchas Horowitz becomes head of the Council of Four Lands
note: R. Pinchas HaLevi Horowitz becoming head of the Va'ad Arba Aratzot.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 225

name: Maharal returns to Prague after four years away
note: Maharal returns to Prague after four years away.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Jews are expelled again from Cochem
note: Jews who had returned to Cochem were expelled again.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Additional German provinces expel Jewish communities
note: Expulsions from a number of German provinces around this time.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Poznań fire kills seventy-six Jews and burns eighty Torah scrolls
note: A major fire in Poznań killed seventy-six Jews and destroyed eighty Torah scrolls; the Jewish quarter was abandoned for two years.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Jews are expelled from Piotrków after a blood libel
note: The expulsion of Piotrków's Jews after a blood-libel accusation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Maharal leaves Prague to become rabbi of Poznań
note: Maharal left Prague and accepted the rabbinate of Poznań.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: R. Mordechai Yaffe becomes rabbi of Prague
note: The author of the Levushim was appointed rabbi in Prague after Maharal's departure.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: R. Elazar Azkiri writes Sefer Charedim in Safed
note: The composition of the mussar work Sefer Charedim is placed in Safed in 1592.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Vilna Jews are attacked and their property is plundered
note: The Jews of Vilna were attacked; houses and shops were plundered.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Many Jews are massacred in Bucharest during a revolt
note: A massacre of Jews in Bucharest during a local revolt against Ottoman rule.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Rodrigo de Castro settles in Hamburg and becomes openly Jewish
note: The Portuguese physician Rodrigo de Castro settled in Hamburg, served royalty and openly returned to Judaism.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Patras Jews are murdered and plundered by sailors
note: Jews in Patras murdered and plundered by sailors from Naples and Sicily.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Jews are expelled from the Duchy of Milan
note: The expulsion of Jews from the wider Milanese province.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Maharal returns to Prague
note: Maharal returned to Prague and resumed a central place in the city's rabbinic life.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: R. Mordechai Yaffe moves from Prague to Poznań
note: With Maharal's return to Prague, R. Mordechai Yaffe took the rabbinic position in Poznań.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: R. Yeshayahu Menachem develops the Heter Iska
note: R. Yeshayahu Menachem, a Kraków rabbi and Council of Four Lands participant, is credited with originating the Heter Iska mechanism.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: R. Yeshayahu Menachem dies
note: R. Yeshayahu Menachem died on 25 Av.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Mordechai Meisel dies and the emperor seizes his estate
note: Mordechai Meisel dies and the emperor seizes his estate.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Jewish sacred books are confiscated and burned in Rome
note: Church authorities in Rome confiscated and burned Jewish sacred books in Shvat.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: Seven Jews are hanged in Mantua
note: Seven Jews hanged in Mantua.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: The Jews of Bzenec are massacred
note: The Jewish community of Bisenz/Bzenec being massacred in Iyar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 226

name: A Jew is killed at Bochnia in a ritual-desecration libel
note: The killing of a Jew in Bochnia after a ritual-desecration accusation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: Maharal of Prague dies
note: R. Yehuda Loew, Maharal of Prague, died on 18 Elul at an advanced age.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: R. David Gans, author of Tzemach David, dies in Prague
note: R. David Gans, disciple of the Rema and author of the historical-chronological Tzemach David, died in Prague.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: R. Yitzchak Chayes dies in Prague
note: Ten days after R. David Gans, R. Yitzchak Chayes, author of Appei Ravrevei, also died in Prague.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: A second major fire displaces Poznań’s Jewish community
note: A second major fire displaces Poznań’s Jewish community.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: Maharsha becomes rabbi of Lublin
note: R. Shmuel Edels (Maharsha), whose commentary became standard alongside the Talmud, became rabbi of Lublin.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: The Sma dies
note: R. Yehoshua Falk, author of Sma on Choshen Mishpat and Derisha/Perisha on the Tur, died on 19 Nisan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: Worms Jews repel an attack on the Jewish quarter
note: The Jews of Worms repelled an attack on the Jewish quarter on the eve of Tisha B'Av.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: Frankfurt Jews are attacked and temporarily forced from the city
note: The Jews of Frankfurt were attacked in Elul and forced to leave the city for a period.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: The Shaloh becomes rabbi of Prague
note: R. Yeshayahu Horowitz (the Shaloh), after years in Frankfurt and other communities, became a rabbi in Prague.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: Maharam Lublin dies
note: R. Meir ben Gedalyah of Lublin, a leading rosh yeshiva and commentator on the Talmud, died in Iyar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: Tosafot Yom Tov commentary on the Mishnah is completed
note: R. Yom Tov Lipmann Heller completed Tosafot Yom Tov on the Mishnah on 22 Cheshvan at age 38.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: A Jew is killed at Sochaczew in a blood libel
note: Another blood-libel killing at Sochaczew.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: R. Shlomo Ephraim Luntschitz (Kli Yakar) dies in Prague
note: The author of Kli Yakar and other works died in Prague on 7 Adar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: The Bach becomes rabbi of Kraków
note: R. Yoel Sirkes (the Bach) became rabbi in Kraków after serving several other communities.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: Poznań Jews are expelled from their temporary settlement outside the city
note: Jews living in a temporary settlement created after earlier fires were expelled from that area.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 227

name: The Shaloh arrives in Jerusalem
note: After leaving Prague following his wife's death, the Shaloh arrived in Jerusalem in Kislev.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: The Shaloh writes Shnei Luchot HaBrit in Jerusalem
note: The Shaloh's major kabbalistic-mussar work Shnei Luchot HaBrit is associated with his Jerusalem period.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: Third edition of Tzena Urena is published
note: Publication of the third edition of Tzena Urena, a widely read Yiddish biblical-midrashic work aimed especially at readers without advanced textual education.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: Fifteen scholars including the Shaloh are arrested in Jerusalem
note: Fifteen scholars were arrested on Shabbat and released after ransom was paid; the Shaloh subsequently moved to Safed and later Tiberias.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: Portuguese recapture of Bahia leads to execution of five openly Jewish Anusim
note: When the Portuguese retook Bahia from the Dutch, five Portuguese Anusim who had become openly Jewish under Dutch rule were captured and killed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: R. Yom Tov Lipmann Heller is imprisoned in Prague
note: Tosafot Yom Tov was imprisoned after being slandered in a dispute over wartime tax assessments. He was released under restrictions and parts of his books were censored.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: Moshe Shmuler is killed at Przemyśl in a ritual-desecration libel
note: Moshe Shmuler killed at Przemyśl after a ritual-desecration accusation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: German troops expel Mantua’s Jews and confiscate their possessions
note: Invading German troops expelled the Jews of Mantua after confiscating their property.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: Eighteen Jewish children in Reggio Emilia are forcibly baptized
note: The forced baptism of eighteen Jewish children in Reggio Emilia.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: Jews of Venice and Prague are forced to attend conversion sermons
note: Compulsory Christian sermons imposed on the Jewish communities of Venice and Prague.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: Dutch Recife permits open Jewish communal life
note: Dutch Recife permits open Jewish communal life.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: Maharam Schiff completes his chidushim on Bava Kama
note: R. Meir Schiff completed his novellæ on tractate Bava Kama in Cheshvan 5391/1630.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: Maharsha dies in Ostrog
note: Maharsha died on 5 Kislev in Ostrog, where he had served as rabbi during his final years.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: Vilna Jews are attacked and their houses ransacked
note: The Jewish community of Vilna was attacked and homes were ransacked.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: R. Eliyahu Baal Shem of Worms dies
note: R. Eliyahu ben Moshe Loanz, known as Eliyahu Baal Shem of Worms, died on 21 Tammuz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: Lublin Jews are attacked after a blood-libel trial
note: An attack on the Jewish community of Lublin after a blood-libel trial, with some Jews killed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 228

name: Brisk Jews are attacked in an anti-Jewish riot
note: An anti-Jewish riot against the Jews of Brisk/Brest-Litovsk.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 229

name: Twenty Jews are tortured in a Łęczyca blood libel; two are publicly killed
note: Twenty Jews were arrested and tortured after a blood-libel accusation at Łęczyca; two were later publicly executed near the synagogue.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 229

name: The Bach dies in Kraków
note: R. Yoel Sirkes, author of Bayit Chadash on the Tur and glosses on the Talmud, died in Kraków on 20 Adar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 229

name: R. Yehoshua Falk becomes rosh yeshiva in Kraków
note: R. Yehoshua ben Yosef Falk became rosh yeshiva in Kraków after the death of R. Natan Shapiro; his major disciple the Shach moved there with him.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 229

name: R. Yitzchak Aboab da Fonseca leaves Amsterdam for Recife
note: R. Yitzchak Aboab da Fonseca leaves Amsterdam for Recife.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 229

name: R. Yitzchak Aboab da Fonseca becomes the first rabbi in the Western Hemisphere
note: R. Yitzchak Aboab da Fonseca becomes the first rabbi in the Western Hemisphere.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 229

name: Yehuda HaMa’amin is burned by the Spanish Inquisition after converting to Judaism
note: The Spanish nobleman Lope de Vera y Alarcón adopted Judaism in prison, circumcised himself, took the name Yehuda HaMa'amin and was burned after refusing to renounce Judaism.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 229

name: Mogilev Jews are attacked during Tashlich
note: An armed mob including the mayor attacked Jews at the river during Tashlich on Rosh Hashanah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 229

name: Taz publishes Turei Zahav on Yoreh De’ah
note: R. David HaLevi (Taz) published Turei Zahav on the Yoreh De'ah section of the Shulchan Aruch, one of the commentaries that helped define the code's later authoritative form.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 229

name: Shach publishes Siftei Kohen on Yoreh De’ah
note: Shach publishes Siftei Kohen on Yoreh De’ah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 229

name: R. Yitzchak de Castro Tartas is burned in Lisbon
note: R. Yitzchak de Castro Tartas was burned alive in Lisbon for teaching Judaism to Anusim in Portuguese Brazil.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 229

name: Khmelnytsky uprising devastates Jewish communities across Ukraine and Poland-Lithuania
note: Khmelnytsky uprising devastates Jewish communities across Ukraine and Poland-Lithuania.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: Nemyriv massacre kills thousands of Jews
note: About 6,000 Jews killed at Nemyriv on 20 Sivan, a date later associated with communal fasting and mourning.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: About one thousand Jews are tortured and killed at Tulchyn
note: About one thousand Jews tortured and killed at Tulchyn on 4 Tammuz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: Polonne massacre kills thousands including R. Shimshon of Ostropole
note: About 10,000 Jews killed at Polonne on 3 Av, including the kabbalistic preacher R. Shimshon of Ostropole.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: Thousands of Jews are killed at Starokostiantyniv on Tisha B’Av
note: About 3,000 Jewish deaths at Starokostiantyniv, including refugees who had sought shelter there.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: R. Naftali Katz is killed by Khmelnytsky’s forces
note: R. Naftali, a descendant by marriage of Maharal's family, was killed on 5 Tishrei by forces associated with the uprising.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: Thousands of Jews are killed at Dubno
note: Thousands of Jews are killed at Dubno.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: Narol massacre kills local Jews and large numbers of refugees
note: 12,000 Jews killed or drowned in Narol and a further enormous body of refugees killed in the surrounding area.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: Medzhybizh Jews escape Khmelnytsky forces and establish Mordechai Purim
note: The Medzhybizh Jewish community being saved through the efforts of a man named Mordechai and his wife Esther; the community instituted a local Purim on 12 Tevet.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: The parents of the future Magen Avraham are killed in the massacres
note: The parents of R. Avraham Abele Gombiner, later the Magen Avraham, among the victims of the 1648 massacres.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: The Taz flees Ostrog and takes refuge in a fortress
note: R. David HaLevi (Taz) fled Ostrog during the Cossack violence and sought refuge in a fortress.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: Jewish refugees flee toward Romania, Hungary, Moldavia and Transylvania
note: The upheaval produced a large refugee movement out of the devastated Polish-Ukrainian regions toward neighbouring lands.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: Prague’s Jews receive a banner for helping defend the city against Swedish forces
note: At the end of the Thirty Years' War, Prague's Jews were presented with a banner in recognition of their role in defending the city against Swedish invaders.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 230

name: Ninety-six Anusim are burned by the Inquisition in Mexico
note: Ninety-six Marranos/Anusim burned to death in Mexico.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Cossack forces kill many Jews in Iași
note: Many Jews killed in Jassy/Iași by Cossack forces in the aftermath of the Khmelnytsky-era upheavals.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Council of Four Lands establishes the 20 Sivan fast for the 1648 massacres
note: The Va'ad Arba Aratzot proclaimed 20 Sivan as a communal fast commemorating the Khmelnytsky massacres.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Council of Lithuania institutes three years of memorial mourning
note: The Va'ad Medinat Lita instituted a three-year period of communal mourning after the massacres, including restrictions such as music at weddings.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: A Jew is killed at Kadaň in a blood libel and the community is expelled
note: A blood-libel killing in Kadan/Kadaň followed by expulsion of the remaining Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Cossack and Tatar forces kill many Jews in Bar
note: Many Jews were killed in Bar by Cossack and Tatar forces.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: David ben Chaim is burned to death in Pidhaitsi
note: David ben Chaim is burned to death in Pidhaitsi.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Manuel Fernandes de Villareal is executed by the Portuguese Inquisition
note: The Portuguese diplomat Manuel Fernandes de Villareal was discovered to be secretly Jewish and executed by the Inquisition during Chanukah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Relatives of Manuel Fernandes de Villareal become openly Jewish in Livorno
note: Relatives of Manuel Fernandes de Villareal become openly Jewish in Livorno.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Another Cossack attack kills many Jews in Iași
note: Another major attack on the Jews of Jassy/Iași by invading Cossacks.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: The Taz becomes rabbi of Lviv
note: After years of displacement following the 1648 massacres, R. David HaLevi, the Taz, became rabbi of Lemberg/Lviv and participated in the Council of Four Lands.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Tosafot Yom Tov dies in Kraków
note: R. Yom Tov Lipmann Heller, author of Tosafot Yom Tov, died in Elul while serving in Kraków.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: R. Yehoshua Heschel succeeds Tosafot Yom Tov in Kraków
note: R. Yehoshua Heschel, formerly rosh yeshiva and rabbi in Lublin, succeeded Tosafot Yom Tov as rabbi of Kraków.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Portuguese reconquest of Recife drives its Jewish community into exile
note: When Portugal reconquered Recife from the Dutch, the open Jewish community fled; many went to the Netherlands.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Twenty-three Jewish refugees from Recife settle in New Amsterdam
note: Twenty-three Sephardic refugees from Dutch Brazil reached New Amsterdam, joining other Jewish arrivals and forming the nucleus of what became New York's first lasting Jewish community.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Governor Stuyvesant resists the settlement of Jews in New Amsterdam
note: Peter Stuyvesant did not readily accept the Jewish refugees. Dutch West India Company directors ultimately required that they be allowed to remain under conditions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Avraham Nunez Bernal is burned in Córdoba after openly affirming Judaism
note: Avraham Nunez Bernal is burned in Córdoba after openly affirming Judaism.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: A nephew of Avraham Nunez Bernal is also burned
note: Bernal's nephew was burned within a few months of him.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Russian and Swedish invasions devastate Polish Jewish communities
note: Broad Jewish losses during the Russian and Swedish invasions of Poland that followed the Khmelnytsky catastrophe.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Russian forces capture Vilna and kill large numbers of Jews
note: Russian forces capture Vilna and kill large numbers of Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: The Shach flees Vilna
note: R. Shabbetai HaKohen, the Shach, fled Vilna during the invasion.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: R. Moshe Rivkes flees Vilna and temporarily settles in Amsterdam
note: R. Moshe Rivkes, later author of Be'er HaGolah on the Shulchan Aruch, escaped Vilna and was allowed to remain for a time in Amsterdam.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: R. Ephraim HaKohen flees Vilna
note: R. Ephraim HaKohen, later author of Sha'ar Ephraim, fled Vilna with his family.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: R. Yaakov Sak survives the Vilna fighting and escapes
note: R. Yaakov Sak was left for dead during the fighting but survived and escaped.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 237

name: Swedish forces capture Kraków and many Jews flee
note: Swedish occupation of Kraków drove many Jews away, including refugees who had already fled the Khmelnytsky massacres and the Thirty Years' War.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Jews remaining in Kraków suffer under Swedish occupation and Polish resistance
note: Severe suffering among Jews who remained during the two-year Swedish occupation and the Polish counteroffensive.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: One hundred fifty Jews of Chmielnik are killed after being accused of aiding Sweden
note: Polish resistance forces killed about 150 Jews of Chmielnik after accusing them of helping the Swedish army.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: The parents of R. Shabbetai Bass are killed at Kalisz
note: The parents of the future bibliographer and printer R. Shabbetai Bass were killed in Kalisz during the Polish-Swedish war.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Mogilev’s Jews are massacred as Polish forces counterattack
note: Jews who had been living under Russian occupation were massacred as Polish forces approached to retake Mogilev.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Thousands of Jews are killed in Lublin
note: Thousands of Jewish deaths in Lublin on 14 Tishrei during the continuing wars.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: The Shach flees Lublin for Moravia
note: After escaping Vilna and then Lublin, the Shach fled to Moravia and eventually became rabbi in Holešov.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: R. Aharon Shmuel Kaidanover flees after his daughters are killed in Lublin
note: Kaidanover fled after his two young daughters were killed in Lublin; he later became rabbi in Mikulov.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Most Jews of Sandomierz are killed and the survivors expelled
note: The destruction of most of the Sandomierz Jewish community and expulsion of survivors.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Most Jews of Tarnobrzeg are killed and the survivors expelled
note: The destruction of most of the Tarnobrzeg Jewish community and expulsion of survivors.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Jews resume open residence in England
note: After years of advocacy by Menasseh ben Israel and the practical recognition that no English law barred Jewish residence, Jews were able to live openly in England under Cromwell's Protectorate.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Three hundred fifty Jewish families are killed at Krotoszyn
note: The killing of 350 Jewish families at Krotoszyn during the Polish war against Sweden.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Two hundred Jewish families are killed at Opatów
note: 200 Jewish families killed in Apta/Opatów.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: One hundred Jewish families are killed at Brześć Kujawski
note: 100 Jewish families killed at Brześć Kujawski.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Fifty Jewish families are killed at Cieszanów
note: 50 Jewish families killed at Cheshanov/Cieszanów.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Forty Jewish families are killed at Brzeziny
note: 40 Jewish families killed at Brzeziny.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: One hundred fifty Jews are killed at Chęciny
note: 150 Jews killed at Chęciny.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Amsterdam’s rabbis place Baruch Spinoza in cherem
note: At age 24, Baruch Spinoza was formally excommunicated by the Portuguese Jewish community of Amsterdam after refusing to retract views judged heretical.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Polish recapture of Łęczyca kills thousands of Jews
note: About 3,000 Jews killed when Polish forces recaptured Łęczyca from Sweden and says some sources reported 600 Torah scrolls burned.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Three Jews are killed in Kraków on the eve of Shavuot
note: Three Jewish deaths in Kraków on Erev Shavuot.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Hundreds of Jews are killed in Kalisz at the end of the Swedish war
note: Hundreds of Jewish deaths in Kalisz as the Swedish war ended.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: Eight Jews are killed in Przemyśl
note: Eight Jews were killed in Przemyśl in Nisan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 238

name: R. Yisrael ben Shalom and R. Tuvyah Bachrach are killed at Ruzhany in a blood libel
note: The two rabbis were killed at Ruzhany on Rosh Hashanah after a blood-libel accusation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Russian capture of Bykhaw kills about three hundred Jews
note: Approximately 300 Jewish deaths when Russian forces captured Bykhaw in Tevet.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: The Shach meets the young Magen Avraham in Kalisz
note: A meeting in Kalisz between the Shach and R. Avraham Abele Gombiner, later the Magen Avraham.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: R. Ephraim HaKohen becomes rabbi in Buda
note: After fleeing Vilna, R. Ephraim HaKohen became rabbi in Buda, accompanied by his son-in-law R. Yaakov Sak.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Chacham Tzvi is born into the refugee rabbinic family in Buda
note: The newborn grandson accompanying R. Ephraim HaKohen is identified as the future Chacham Tzvi.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: R. Menachem Mendel Krochmal dies in Mikulov
note: R. Menachem Mendel Krochmal, author of Tzemach Tzedek I and provincial rabbi of Moravia, died on 2 Shevat.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Persian Jews are permitted to resume open Jewish practice
note: Persian Jews are permitted to resume open Jewish practice.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Cochin’s Jews flee Portuguese attacks and plunder
note: The Jews of Cochin fled when Portuguese authorities attacked them and plundered their property, blaming them in the context of Dutch attempts to conquer the area.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Cochin’s Jews return after the Dutch conquest
note: The Jewish community returned when Dutch forces successfully conquered Cochin the following year.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Mattityahu Kalahora is tortured, dismembered and burned in Kraków
note: The Jewish physician Mattityahu Kalahora was executed in Kraków after being accused of blasphemy against Christianity.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Cossack invasion massacres Jews in Bratslav
note: Many Jews were massacred in Bratslav during a Cossack invasion.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Anti-Jewish riots in Lviv kill many Jews including two sons of the Taz
note: Many Jews killed in Lviv riots in Iyar, including R. Mordechai and R. Shlomo, sons of the Taz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Isaac Newton helps establish a new empirical style of scientific investigation
note: Newton as a wider-world milestone, emphasizing systematic observation and the new scientific method that accompanied early modern science.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Shabbetai Tzvi publicly proclaims himself Messiah
note: Shabbetai Tzvi's public messianic proclamation is placed in Eretz Yisrael in Sivan, with crucial support from Nathan of Gaza.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Nathan of Gaza becomes the prophetic advocate of Shabbetai Tzvi
note: Nathan of Gaza proclaimed prophetic support for Shabbetai Tzvi and became a major engine of the movement's rapid spread.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Sabbatean messianic enthusiasm spreads across the Jewish world
note: Reports, letters, rumors and messianic expectations carried Shabbetai Tzvi's movement through Jewish communities across Europe, the Ottoman world, North Africa and the Middle East.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Shabbetai Tzvi returns to Izmir and mobilizes a mass following
note: In his home city of Izmir, Shabbetai Tzvi generated intense public enthusiasm through charismatic preaching and prayer.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 239

name: Ottoman authorities arrest Shabbetai Tzvi on his journey to Constantinople
note: Shabbetai Tzvi was arrested by Ottoman authorities while travelling toward Constantinople.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: The Taz sends his son and stepson to investigate Shabbetai Tzvi
note: The Taz sent his son and stepson from Poland to investigate Shabbetai Tzvi. They returned impressed, and Shabbetai sent a silk garment to honor the Taz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: A Tunisian Jew commits suicide during a forced baptism ceremony in Rome
note: A Jew from Tunis disrupting his forced baptism in Rome by taking his own life.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: Shabbetai Tzvi holds court-like audiences while imprisoned at Gallipoli
note: While detained in the fortress at Gallipoli, Shabbetai Tzvi received followers and delegations, which strengthened his messianic prestige.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: Shabbetai Tzvi converts to Islam at Edirne
note: Brought before the Ottoman authorities and faced with death or conversion, Shabbetai Tzvi converted to Islam in Elul 1666.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: Some Sabbatean followers convert to Islam after Shabbetai Tzvi’s apostasy
note: Some followers imitated Shabbetai's conversion, while others developed interpretations that preserved belief in his messianic mission.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: Tatar invasion massacres the Jews of Pidhaitsi
note: The Jewish community of Podhajce/Pidhaitsi massacred during a Tatar invasion.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: Rome ends the annual humiliating Carnival races imposed on Jews
note: 1667 as the last year Jews were compelled to participate in humiliating Carnival races in Rome.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: The Taz dies three years after the Lviv riots
note: Retrospectively in the 1664 entry that the Taz died three years after the riots in which two of his sons were killed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: Jews are expelled from parts of Morocco
note: Expulsions of Jews from several parts of Morocco.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: R. Raphael Levi is burned at Metz after a blood libel
note: R. Raphael Levi was burned to death at Metz after a blood-libel accusation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: The Habsburg monarchy expels Jews from Austria
note: A major expulsion removed Jews from Austria, including refugees who had previously arrived after the 1648 massacres.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: The last Jews leave Vienna on Tisha B’Av
note: The final departure of Vienna's Jews in the 1670 expulsion is dated to Tisha B'Av.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: Fifty wealthy Jewish families are permitted to settle in Brandenburg
note: Fifty wealthy families received permission to settle in Brandenburg; some later established themselves in Berlin.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: R. Gershon Ashkenazi leaves Vienna and becomes rabbi of Metz
note: R. Gershon Ashkenazi was among those expelled from Vienna and subsequently became rabbi in Metz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: R. Avraham Abele Gombiner completes the Magen Avraham
note: Completion of the Magen Avraham, the influential commentary on Orach Chayim of the Shulchan Aruch.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 240

name: R. Reuven Katz, author of Yalkut Reuveni, dies in Prague
note: The Prague scholar R. Reuven Katz, author of Yalkut Reuveni, died.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: R. Chaim Benveniste dies in Izmir
note: R. Chaim Benveniste, author of Knesset HaGedolah on the Shulchan Aruch, died in Izmir on 19 Elul.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: R. Aharon Shmuel Kaidanover dies during a rabbinic gathering
note: Kaidanover died on 19 Tammuz while attending a rabbinic gathering at Chmielnik.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: Shabbetai Tzvi dies in exile at Ulcinj
note: Shabbetai Tzvi died on Yom Kippur in Dulcigno/Ulcinj, where Ottoman authorities had exiled him.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: Sabbatean groups survive Shabbetai Tzvi’s death as secret sects
note: After his death, Sabbatean communities and clandestine circles persisted for generations in the Ottoman world, Italy and Poland-Lithuania.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: Four Jews are killed in Kraków
note: Four Jews killed in Kraków.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: A plague kills about one thousand Jews in Kazimierz
note: About 1,000 Jewish deaths from plague in Kazimierz, the Jewish district of Kraków.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: Jews are expelled from Yemen after synagogues are destroyed
note: A general expulsion of Yemenite Jews after many synagogues had already been demolished.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: Yemenite Jews are permitted to return after the exile
note: Yemenite Jews are permitted to return after the exile.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: A plague kills more than three thousand Jews in Prague
note: More than 3,000 Jewish deaths in Prague during a severe plague.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: Anti-Jewish riots kill many Jews in Kraków
note: Anti-Jewish riots in Kraków during Adar with many Jewish deaths.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: The Jewish community of Uherský Brod is massacred
note: The killing of the entire Jewish community of Uherský Brod, including the chronicler R. Natan Nata Hanover.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: R. Natan Nata Hanover is killed at Uherský Brod
note: The author of Yeven Metzula, the major chronicle of the 1648 massacres, was killed during the attack on Uherský Brod.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: Three hundred Sabbateans in Salonika convert to Islam and form a crypto-Sabbatean community
note: A mass conversion of about 300 followers of Shabbetai Tzvi in Salonika. YIVO identifies the later Dönmeh as the major crypto-Jewish Sabbatean community formed after the 1683 conversion.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: Austrian siege of Buda kills many Jews including Chacham Tzvi’s wife and child
note: Many Jews died during the Austrian siege of Buda, including the wife and infant daughter of R. Tzvi Ashkenazi, the Chacham Tzvi.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: Austrian capture of Buda leads to plunder of the Jewish quarter and burning of Torah scrolls
note: After taking Buda, Austrian troops plundered the Jewish quarter and burned Torah scrolls.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: Poznań Jews fight a three-day battle to defend their quarter from rioters
note: The Jews of Poznań successfully resisted anti-Jewish rioters for three days but suffered heavy losses.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: Vilna Jews are attacked and property is damaged
note: Another anti-Jewish riot struck Vilna, damaging Jewish property.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 241

name: Beit Shmuel is printed
note: R. Shmuel ben Uri Shraga Faivish's Beit Shmuel on Even HaEzer was printed as the first book of R. Shabbetai Bass's new press.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: R. Ya’ir Chaim Bacharach flees Worms for Metz during French occupation
note: When French forces occupied Worms, R. Ya'ir Chaim Bacharach fled to Metz; he later returned to Worms.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: R. Menachem Mendel Auerbach dies in Krotoszyn
note: The author of Ateret Zekeinim on the Shulchan Aruch died on 20 Tammuz in Krotoszyn.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: A major fire destroys hundreds of Jewish houses and eleven synagogues in Prague
note: 300 Jewish houses and eleven synagogues destroyed in a Prague fire.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: R. Yosef Shmuel of Kraków becomes rabbi of Frankfurt
note: R. Yosef Shmuel, known for Hagahot HaShas and work on Mesorat HaShas, becoming rabbi of Frankfurt; it notes that he died four years later.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: R. Aharon Teomim is arrested at a Council of Four Lands meeting and dies from beatings
note: R. Aharon Teomim, newly appointed rabbi of Kraków, was arrested without clear cause while attending a Council of Four Lands meeting and died from severe beatings.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: R. Aharon Teomim becomes rabbi of Kraków
note: R. Aharon Teomim had just become rabbi of Kraków after previously serving in Worms, shortly before his arrest and fatal beating at Chmielnik.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: Glikl of Hameln begins writing her memoirs
note: After the death of her first husband, Glikl began the Yiddish memoirs that became an exceptionally rich source on early modern Jewish family, commercial and communal life.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: Pri Chadash is printed in Amsterdam
note: R. Chizkiyah da Silva printed Pri Chadash on the Shulchan Aruch while in Amsterdam on a mission from Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: Fire destroys the Jewish quarter of Brody
note: The destruction by fire of Brody's Jewish section.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: R. Moshe Zacuto dies in Mantua
note: R. Moshe Zacuto (RaMaZ/ReMeZ), an important kabbalist and long-serving Italian rabbi, died in Mantua on the second day of Sukkot.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: The Baal Shem Tov is born
note: The birth of R. Yisrael ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem Tov, is dated to 18 Elul 1698.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: R. Ya’ir Chaim Bacharach returns to Worms as rabbi
note: Retrospectively that Bacharach returned to Worms ten years after his 1689 flight to Metz and became rabbi there.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: R. Yehuda Chasid leads a large migration toward Eretz Yisrael
note: R. Yehuda Chasid travelled through Europe preaching repentance and led a large group of followers toward Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 242

name: R. Yehuda Chasid reaches Jerusalem and dies within days
note: Only a fraction of the original group completed the journey. R. Yehuda Chasid died a few days after reaching Jerusalem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: Lviv gunpowder explosion kills thirty-six Jews including the Pnei Yehoshua’s family
note: Lviv gunpowder explosion kills thirty-six Jews including the Pnei Yehoshua’s family.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: Attack on Bila Tserkva marks the beginning of the Haidamak violence in Codex
note: Attack on Bila Tserkva marks the beginning of the Haidamak violence.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: Hungarian uprising kills and displaces many Jews
note: Jewish deaths and widespread displacement during the unsuccessful Hungarian revolution.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: Anti-Jewish rioters attack and loot Krotoszyn
note: The Jews of Krotoszyn were attacked and their property looted.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: Kalisz fire kills forty-five Jews
note: Forty-five Jewish deaths in a fire at Kalisz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: Russian troops attack Leszno and burn the Jewish quarter
note: Invading Russian troops plundered the Jews of Leszno and burned the town's Jewish section.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: Plague kills about four hundred fifty Jews in Kalisz
note: About 450 Jewish deaths from plague in Kalisz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: Fire destroys Vitebsk’s Jewish quarter
note: Destruction by fire of the Jewish section of Vitebsk.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: Jews of Leszno are blamed for plague and expelled
note: Jews of Leszno are blamed for plague and expelled.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: Jews are expelled from Groningen
note: An expulsion of Jews from Groningen in the northern Netherlands.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: Chacham Tzvi becomes rabbi of Amsterdam’s Ashkenazi community
note: R. Tzvi Ashkenazi became rabbi of Amsterdam's comparatively new Ashkenazi congregation after an earlier period in Altona.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: Adel of Lviv is killed after a blood-libel confession intended to save others
note: Adel, daughter of Moshe Kikinish, being killed after confessing to a blood-libel accusation to save other Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: R. Yechiel Heilprin becomes rabbi of Minsk
note: R. Yechiel Heilprin, later known for Seder HaDorot, became rabbi of Minsk.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 243

name: A fire destroys Frankfurt’s Jewish quarter
note: A fire originating in the home of R. Naftali Katz destroyed the Jewish quarter of Frankfurt.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: R. Naftali Katz is falsely blamed after the Frankfurt fire and leaves the city
note: Although cleared of charges, R. Naftali Katz was maliciously accused of preventing firefighting in order to test amulets and was compelled to leave Frankfurt.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: R. Shabbetai Bass is arrested over accusations against his printing press
note: The author of Siftei Chachamim and pioneer bibliographer was arrested on accusations that his Dyhernfurth press printed anti-Christian material; he was later released.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: R. Eliyahu Shapiro dies in Prague
note: R. Eliyahu Shapiro, author of Eliyahu Rabbah and Eliyahu Zuta on the Levushim, died on 8 Nisan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: R. Yoel Baal Shem dies
note: R. Yoel Baal Shem ben Yitzchak Halpern, a kabbalist associated with the older baalei shem tradition and author of Toldot Adam, died on 4 Tishrei.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: Maharam Esh becomes rabbi of Eisenstadt
note: R. Meir Eisenstadt (Maharam Esh) became rabbi in Eisenstadt after the community recovered from wartime disruption.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: A plague kills 892 Jews in Boskovice
note: 892 Jewish deaths in a plague at Boskovice.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: Poznań’s Jewish community is attacked and many Jews leave
note: After a recent ergot epidemic had already weakened the community, an attack in 1716 prompted many Jews to leave Poznań.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: Chacham Tzvi leaves Amsterdam after a Sabbatean controversy
note: R. Tzvi Ashkenazi left Amsterdam after controversy over his excommunication of a prominent Sabbatean and disputes with the older Sephardic congregation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: Chacham Tzvi becomes rabbi of Lviv and dies shortly afterward
note: After travel through England, Germany and Poland, Chacham Tzvi became rabbi in Lviv shortly before dying there on Rosh Chodesh Iyar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: Pnei Yehoshua succeeds Chacham Tzvi in Lviv
note: R. Yaakov Yehoshua Falk, the Pnei Yehoshua, succeeded Chacham Tzvi as rabbi of Lviv.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: Fire completely destroys Mikulov’s Jewish quarter
note: The entire Jewish quarter of Nikolsburg/Mikulov was destroyed by fire.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: Shimshon Wertheimer organizes funds to rebuild Mikulov
note: The wealthy Viennese shtadlan and scholar Shimshon Wertheimer organized financial aid for rebuilding the Jewish community.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: Budapest Jews are attacked and their homes plundered
note: An attack on the Jews of Buda/Budapest in which homes were looted.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 244

name: The Ashkenazi synagogue in Jerusalem is burned and the community flees
note: Attackers broke into the Ashkenazi synagogue associated with R. Yehuda Chasid, burned Torah scrolls and forced the Ashkenazi Jews to flee Jerusalem. The ruined site became known as the Hurva.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: R. Yeshayahu HaLevi and his family die in a Mogilev fire
