note: R. Yeshayahu HaLevi, grandson of the Taz and author of an early Ba'er Heitev, died with his wife and daughter in a fire while travelling toward Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: R. Yeshayahu HaLevi’s Ba’er Heitev summarizes Orach Chayim commentaries
note: R. Yeshayahu HaLevi’s Ba’er Heitev summarizes Orach Chayim commentaries.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: R. Yehuda of Tykocin writes a Ba’er Heitev on the Shulchan Aruch
note: Another Ba'er Heitev by R. Yehuda ben Shimon of Tykocin, covering all four sections of the Shulchan Aruch.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: R. Zecharyah Mendel of Belz writes a Ba’er Heitev
note: R. Zecharyah Mendel of Belz as author of another Ba'er Heitev, used in later standard editions on Yoreh De'ah and Choshen Mishpat.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: R. Moshe Frankfurter writes a Ba’er Heitev on Choshen Mishpat
note: R. Moshe Frankfurter as another author of a Ba'er Heitev, on Choshen Mishpat.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: R. Yaakov Culi arrives in Constantinople to print his grandfather’s works
note: R. Yaakov Culi came to Constantinople to print the writings of his grandfather R. Moshe ibn Chaviv and became a disciple of R. Yehuda Rosannes.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: R. Yaakov Culi begins the scholarly project that becomes Me’am Lo’ez
note: Culi's Constantinople period is associated with his editing of Mishneh LeMelech and his Ladino Me'am Lo'ez, a work that became highly influential in Sephardic popular Torah education.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: Blood-libel violence strikes the Jews of Iași and synagogues are desecrated
note: The Jews of Iași were attacked after a blood-libel accusation and synagogues were desecrated.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: R. Yehuda Rosannes, author of Mishneh LeMelech, dies in Constantinople
note: R. Yehuda Rosannes died on 22 Nisan. His Mishneh LeMelech became an important commentary on the Rambam's Mishneh Torah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: R. Chaim and R. Yehoshua Reitzes are tortured and burned in Lviv
note: R. Chaim and R. Yehoshua Reitzes are tortured and burned in Lviv.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: Pnei Yehoshua becomes rabbi of Berlin after anti-Sabbatean controversy
note: After leaving Lviv amid controversy over his public excommunication of Sabbateans, the Pnei Yehoshua eventually became rabbi in Berlin.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: Ramchal faces suspicion over mystical writings and Sabbatean influence
note: The young R. Moshe Chaim Luzzatto was suspected of Sabbatean influence because of his mystical writings and undertook to stop certain kabbalistic writing under communal pressure.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 245

name: R. Yaakov Reischer dies in Metz
note: R. Yaakov Reischer, author of Shvut Yaakov, Minchat Yaakov and Chok Yaakov, died on 10 Tevet.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 246

name: Simla Chadasha and Tevuot Shor are published
note: R. Alexander Sender Schorr published Simla Chadasha on shechita together with his commentary Tevuot Shor.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 246

name: Haidamak bands massacre twenty-seven Jews at Korsun
note: Twenty-seven Jews massacred by roaming Haidamak bands at Korsun.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 246

name: The Baal Shem Tov begins teaching publicly
note: The Baal Shem Tov's emergence as a public teacher of Chasidut is dated to 1734, after years of association with itinerant hidden pietists.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 246

name: Pnei Yehoshua succeeds R. Yaakov Reischer as rabbi of Metz
note: Pnei Yehoshua succeeded R. Yaakov Reischer in Metz one year after Reischer's 1733 death.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 246

name: Haidamak bands intensify attacks across Polish Ukraine
note: Haidamak bands intensify attacks across Polish Ukraine.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 246

name: Thirty-five Jews are massacred at Pavoloch
note: Thirty-five Jewish deaths at Pavoloch in Haidamak violence.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 246

name: Fourteen Jews are massacred at Pohrebyshche
note: Fourteen Jewish deaths at Pogrebishche/Pohrebyshche in Haidamak violence.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 246

name: Poznań Jews are imprisoned and tortured in a blood libel
note: Many Jews were imprisoned and tortured in a Poznań blood-libel case, further weakening the community.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 246

name: Jews are tortured and killed at Jarosław in a blood libel
note: Multiple Jews tortured and killed at Jarosław after a blood-libel accusation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 246

name: Joseph Süß Oppenheimer is executed at Stuttgart
note: Joseph Süß Oppenheimer is executed at Stuttgart.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 246

name: Baruch Leibov and Alexander Voznitzyn are burned in Saint Petersburg for adopting Judaism
note: Baruch Leibov and the Russian naval officer Alexander Voznitzyn tortured and burned after Leibov introduced Voznitzyn to Judaism.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 246

name: Codex links the year 5500 with the opening of the 'gates of wisdom' and the rise of modern science
note: A Zoharic prediction concerning the year 5500 is associated with the acceleration of science, technology and the Industrial Revolution.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: Or HaChayim arrives in Eretz Yisrael
note: R. Chaim ibn Attar left Morocco because of persecution and famine, travelled through Algiers and Italy, and arrived with followers in Eretz Yisrael. He initially stayed in Acre because of plague in Jerusalem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: R. Yonatan Eybeschutz is appointed rabbi of Metz
note: R. Yonatan Eybeschutz, author of Kereti u-Peleti and Urim ve-Tummim, was appointed rabbi of Metz after the Pnei Yehoshua left.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: Jews are expelled from most of the Russian Empire
note: A broad expulsion of Jews from most of the territory then considered Russia.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: R. David Frankel becomes rabbi of Berlin
note: R. David Frankel, author of Korban HaEidah on the Jerusalem Talmud, was appointed rabbi of Berlin.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: Jews are massacred at Roudnice
note: A massacre of a number of Jews at Roudnice in Bohemia.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: Jews are expelled from Prague under Maria Theresa's decree
note: Jews are expelled from Prague under Maria Theresa's decree.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: R. Shneur Zalman is born
note: The birth of R. Shneur Zalman, later founder of Chabad Hasidism and author of Tanya and Shulchan Aruch HaRav, is dated to 18 Elul.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: Jews are expelled from Buda
note: Maria Theresa's anti-Jewish policy was extended to Buda, where the Jewish community was expelled.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: Ramchal dies in Acre during a plague
note: R. Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, author of Mesillat Yesharim and other works, died in Acre on 26 Iyar during a plague.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: Plague kills many Jews in Safed
note: Many Jews in Safed died in the same regional plague.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: Five Jews are killed at Izyaslav in a blood libel
note: Five Jewish victims of a blood-libel episode at Izyaslav.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: R. Avraham Gershon of Kitev leaves Europe for Eretz Yisrael
note: At the request of his brother-in-law the Baal Shem Tov, R. Avraham Gershon of Kitev left Europe to settle in Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 247

name: Jews are killed in Breslau riots after a gunpowder-store explosion
note: Jewish deaths in riots that followed the explosion of a gunpowder storehouse in Breslau.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: R. Yonatan Eybeschutz becomes rabbi of Hamburg-Altona-Wandsbek
note: R. Yonatan Eybeschutz became rabbi of the united communities of Hamburg, Altona and Wandsbek.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: The Emden–Eybeschutz controversy erupts over amulets
note: During a period of high maternal mortality, Eybeschutz wrote amulets. R. Yaakov Emden later opened some and alleged Sabbatean content, triggering a prolonged international controversy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: Eleven Jews are killed at Zhytomyr in a blood libel
note: Eleven Jews killed, with thirteen others forced to convert to Christianity, in a blood-libel case at Zhytomyr.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: Thirteen Jews at Zhytomyr are forcibly converted after the blood libel
note: Thirteen Jews were forced to convert to Christianity in the Zhytomyr blood-libel episode.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: Council of Four Lands scholars clear R. Yonatan Eybeschutz of suspicion
note: At Yaroslav on 3 Cheshvan, scholars of the Council of Four Lands formally cleared Eybeschutz of suspicion in the amulet controversy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: Noda BiYehuda becomes rabbi of Prague and Bohemia
note: R. Yechezkel Landau, author of Noda BiYehuda, became rabbi of Prague and chief rabbinic authority of Bohemia.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: Pnei Yehoshua leaves Frankfurt after taking Emden's side in the Eybeschutz controversy
note: After a decade in Frankfurt, the Pnei Yehoshua left amid controversy after supporting R. Yaakov Emden.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: Fire destroys most of Prague's Jewish quarter and many writings of R. Eliyahu Shapiro
note: A major fire destroyed most of the Jewish section of Prague and burned many manuscripts associated with R. Eliyahu Shapiro.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: Hertzl Levi is killed at Colmar after a libel trial
note: Hertzl Levi killed in Colmar following a libel trial.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: Yaakov ben Pinchas and Wolf Winkler are killed in a Poznań blood libel
note: The deaths of community trustee Yaakov ben Pinchas and Wolf Winkler in a blood-libel episode at Poznań.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: R. Aryeh Leib Kalahora is killed in the Poznań blood-libel persecution
note: R. Aryeh Leib ben Yosef Kalahora, the darshan, was killed on 18 Kislev only weeks after the earlier victims.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: R. Yitzchak Lampronti dies in Ferrara
note: R. Yitzchak Lampronti, rabbi, rosh yeshiva, physician and author of the encyclopedic Pachad Yitzchak, died in Ferrara.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: Jacob Frank re-emerges in Poland as leader of a Sabbatean-derived movement
note: After years in the Ottoman world among Sabbatean circles, Jacob Frank became a leader among secret Sabbatean followers in Poland and urged them toward public expression.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 248

name: A cherem against Frank's followers is proclaimed at Brody
note: A cherem against Frank's followers is proclaimed at Brody.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 249

name: Frankists and traditional Jews hold a disputation at Kamianets-Podilskyi
note: The local bishop organized a public disputation in which Frankist speakers attacked the Talmud.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 249

name: Talmud volumes are confiscated and burned at Kamianets-Podilskyi
note: Following the disputation, the bishop ordered copies of the Talmud confiscated and burned.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 249

name: Jewish books are burned at Lviv in the Frankist campaign
note: Jewish books burned at Lviv as part of the wider anti-Talmud campaign associated with the Frankists.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 249

name: Jewish books are burned at Zhovkva in the Frankist campaign
note: Jewish books burned at Zhovkva as part of the anti-Talmud campaign.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 249

name: Jewish books are burned at Brody in the Frankist campaign
note: Jewish books burned at Brody during the anti-Talmud campaign.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 249

name: Frankists support blood-libel allegations in the Lviv disputation
note: At the 1759 Lviv disputation, Frankist representatives supported the false claim that Jews used Christian blood for ritual purposes.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 249

name: R. Chaim Rappaport leads the traditional Jewish side in the Lviv disputation
note: R. Chaim Rappaport leads the traditional Jewish side in the Lviv disputation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 249

name: Thousands of Frank's followers undergo baptism after the Lviv disputation
note: After the disputation, large numbers of Frank's followers entered Christianity, while many continued secret or heterodox beliefs.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 249

name: Jacob Frank is imprisoned at Częstochowa
note: Christian authorities arrested Jacob Frank amid suspicions that his conversion was insincere and his movement heretical; he remained confined for years.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 249

name: Safed earthquake kills about two hundred Jews and prompts emigration
note: About 200 Jewish deaths in a Safed earthquake; many survivors began leaving the town.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 249

name: The Baal Shem Tov dies in Medzhybizh
note: The Baal Shem Tov dies in Medzhybizh.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 249

name: Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezritsh, becomes the central leader of Hasidism
note: After the Besht's death, Dov Ber of Mezritsh became the movement's most influential organizing leader, although other Besht disciples also maintained independent circles.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Hasidism expands through disciples of the Besht in Poland and Eastern Europe
note: The Besht's movement as a mass spiritual reorientation in communities still recovering from the seventeenth-century massacres and Sabbatean crisis.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Jews are expelled from Courland
note: A general expulsion of Jews from Courland.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Many Jews are killed at Mohyliv-Podilskyi
note: Many Jewish deaths at Mogilev-Podolski.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Jews are killed at Wojsławice in a Frankist-supported blood libel
note: A number of Jews were killed in a blood-libel case at Wojsławice in which Frankist influence played a role.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Anti-Jewish riots strike Emden
note: The Jews of Emden were attacked in anti-Jewish riots in Sivan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Four Jews are killed at Kalisz in a blood libel
note: Four Jewish victims of a blood-libel episode in Kalisz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: The Polish government dissolves the Council of Four Lands
note: The Va'ad Arba Aratzot was discontinued as the Polish government reduced Jewish communal autonomy and changed tax-collection methods.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: R. Yonatan Eybeschutz dies
note: R. Yonatan Eybeschutz died on 21 Elul after decades of rabbinic leadership and the long amulet controversy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: R. Yitzchak Horowitz becomes rabbi of Hamburg
note: R. Yitzchak Horowitz, known as Reb Itzikel me-Hamburg, was appointed with R. Yaakov Emden's approval and later helped restore dignity after the Eybeschutz controversy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: R. Nachman of Horodenka settles in Eretz Yisrael
note: R. Nachman of Horodenka and other disciples of the Baal Shem Tov settled in Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Leszno fire kills twenty Jews and destroys the Jewish quarter
note: A fire destroyed the entire Jewish section of Leszno and killed twenty Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Yad Malachi is published
note: R. Malachi HaKohen published Yad Malachi, a work on principles and methods of Talmudic and halachic study.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: R. Shneur Zalman becomes maggid in Liozna
note: Retrospectively that R. Shneur Zalman had been appointed maggid in his home town of Liozna in 1767.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: Haidamak violence sweeps Jewish towns in Polish Ukraine
note: Renewed Haidamak massacres across multiple Jewish towns, culminating in the catastrophe at Uman.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Haidamaks attack Jews at Fastiv
note: This locality among the towns devastated during the 1768 Haidamak massacres.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Haidamaks attack Jews at Lysianka
note: This locality among the towns devastated during the 1768 Haidamak massacres.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Haidamaks attack Jews at Zhabotyn
note: This locality among the towns devastated during the 1768 Haidamak massacres.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Haidamaks attack Jews at Kaniv
note: This locality among the towns devastated during the 1768 Haidamak massacres.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Haidamaks attack Jews at Tetiiv
note: This locality among the towns devastated during the 1768 Haidamak massacres.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Haidamaks attack Jews at Korsun
note: This locality among the towns devastated during the 1768 Haidamak massacres.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Haidamaks attack Jews and refugees at Balta
note: This locality among the towns devastated during the 1768 Haidamak massacres.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Jewish defenders at Uman are overwhelmed and thousands are massacred
note: Jewish defenders at Uman are overwhelmed and thousands are massacred.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: R. Netanel Weil dies in Karlsruhe
note: R. Netanel Weil, author of Korban Netanel on the Rosh, died in Karlsruhe.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Metzudat David and Metzudat Tzion are completed and printed
note: R. Yechiel Hillel Altschuler completed and printed his father's biblical commentaries Metzudat David and Metzudat Tzion.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: R. Shneur Zalman begins writing Shulchan Aruch HaRav
note: At the request of the Maggid of Mezritsh, Shneur Zalman began a synthesized halachic code incorporating major post-Shulchan-Aruch opinions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 253

name: Plague kills about eight hundred Jews in Zhovkva
note: Approximately 800 Jewish deaths in a plague at Zhovkva.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: Opponents and Hasidim hold a public debate at Shklov
note: A public debate on the Hasidic movement was organized by opponents. Hasidim were represented by Shneur Zalman and R. Avraham of Kalisk.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: Vilna beit din proclaims a cherem against Hasidim
note: After the Shklov debate failed to resolve tensions, a formal excommunication against Hasidim was proclaimed in Vilna and circulated widely.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: Persecution of Hasidim intensifies after the Vilna cherem
note: The circulated excommunication led to social and communal persecution of Hasidim in multiple communities.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: Shneur Zalman and Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk unsuccessfully seek a meeting with the Vilna Gaon
note: Shneur Zalman and Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk unsuccessfully seek a meeting with the Vilna Gaon.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: First Partition of Poland transforms the political setting of East European Jewry
note: Austria, Prussia and Russia partitioned large parts of Poland-Lithuania, bringing huge Jewish populations under new imperial regimes.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: Jacob Frank is released from Częstochowa imprisonment after the partition
note: Russian annexation brought the fortress holding Jacob Frank under new control and he was released.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: The Maggid of Mezritsh dies
note: Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezritsh, central organizer of second-generation Hasidism, died on 19 Kislev.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: R. Aharon of Karlin dies
note: R. Aharon of Karlin, one of the Maggid's major disciples and a powerful early Hasidic leader, died about half a year before the Maggid.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: R. Meir Teomim dies in Lviv
note: R. Meir Teomim died in Lviv.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: R. Yosef Teomim returns from Berlin to succeed his father in Lviv
note: R. Yosef Teomim, later author of Pri Megadim, came from Berlin to succeed his father in Lviv.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: Frankist followers convert to Christianity at Prostějov
note: A group of Jacob Frank's followers converting at Prossnitz/Prostějov.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: Maria Theresa expels Jews from Hodonín
note: A local expulsion of Jews from Hodonín in Moravia.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 254

name: R. Yaakov Emden dies
note: R. Yaakov Emden, author of She'ilat Ya'avetz and one of the central opponents of alleged Sabbateanism in his generation, died on Rosh Chodesh Iyar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: Jewish supporters of the American Revolution flee British-occupied New York
note: Many Jews loyal to the American Revolution leaving New York during British occupation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk leads more than three hundred Hasidim to Eretz Yisrael
note: A large group led by R. Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, including R. Avraham of Kalisk, emigrated to Eretz Yisrael, establishing an enduring Hasidic presence in Safed and Tiberias.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: R. Shalom Sharabi dies in Jerusalem
note: R. Shalom Sharabi, kabbalist and rosh yeshiva in Jerusalem, died.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: Jews are expelled from Kitzingen
note: The expulsion of Jews from Kitzingen.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: A modern Jewish school is operating in Berlin
note: Retrospectively that a Berlin school emphasizing modern education was already in existence by 1778, an important part of the institutional spread of Haskalah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 256

name: R. Elchanan Ashkenazi dies near Gdańsk
note: R. Elchanan ben Shmuel Ashkenazi, author of Sidrei Taharah, died in the Danzig/Gdańsk area.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: R. Moshe Margolis dies in Brody while seeking funds to print Pnei Moshe
note: The author of Pnei Moshe on the Jerusalem Talmud died in Brody while travelling to secure funding for further printing.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: R. Yitzchak Aisik Taub becomes rabbi in Kalliv
note: The Kalliver Rebbe, a disciple of R. Shmelke of Nikolsburg and R. Elimelech of Lizhensk, became rabbi in Kalliv.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: Vilna proclaims a new cherem against Hasidim
note: A renewed excommunication against Hasidim, again associated with the Vilna Gaon, intensified opposition to the movement.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: Toldot Yaakov Yosef is publicly burned
note: The first published Hasidic book, Toldot Yaakov Yosef, was publicly burned as a consequence of the renewed anti-Hasidic campaign.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: R. Yechiel Michel of Zlotchov leaves Brody under anti-Hasidic pressure
note: The renewed persecution forced R. Yechiel Michel of Zlotchov to leave Brody.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: R. Shlomo of Karlin leaves Karlin under anti-Hasidic pressure
note: R. Shlomo of Karlin left his community under the pressure generated by the renewed cherem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: R. Levi Yitzchak leaves his rabbinate in Pinsk under anti-Hasidic pressure
note: R. Levi Yitzchak, later famed as the Berditchever, left his position in Pinsk after anti-Hasidic opposition.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: R. Natan Adler leaves Frankfurt to become rabbi in Boskovice
note: After controversy over his private congregation and kabbalistic practice, R. Natan Adler left Frankfurt for the rabbinate of Boskovice.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: R. Natan Adler and the young Chasam Sofer visit the Noda BiYehuda in Prague
note: On the journey from Frankfurt, R. Natan Adler and his disciple R. Moshe Sofer were received by the Noda BiYehuda in Prague.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 255

name: Joseph II eases some Austrian restrictions on Jews
note: Partial relief of restrictions in the Habsburg lands under Joseph II.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 256

name: Austrian Jewish communities are required to establish German-language schooling
note: Jewish communities were directed to establish German-language schools or send children to general schools.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 256

name: Hebrew and Yiddish are banned from Austrian Jewish business and communal records
note: Restrictions on the use of Hebrew and Yiddish in business and communal recordkeeping.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 256

name: Moses Mendelssohn publishes his German Bible translation and Biur
note: Mendelssohn's German translation and commentary became an important cultural marker in the emergence of the Haskalah.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 256

name: Haskalah ideology expands around integration, German language and secular study
note: Mendelssohn's program of integration, German-language culture and increased secular study as foundational to the Jewish Enlightenment.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 256

name: Shaagat Aryeh dies in Metz
note: R. Aryeh Leib Gunzberg, author of Shaagat Aryeh, died in Metz after roughly twenty years as rabbi.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 256

name: R. Elimelech of Lizhensk dies
note: R. Elimelech of Lizhensk, one of the Maggid's most influential disciples and a central architect of Polish-Galician Hasidism, died on 21 Adar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 256

name: United States Constitution establishes a federal framework without religious tests
note: United States Constitution establishes a federal framework without religious tests.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 256

name: Austrian Jews are compelled to adopt German-style family names
note: A requirement that Jews in Austria choose German-sounding names from prepared lists.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 256

name: R. Aryeh Leib Heller becomes rabbi of Stryi
note: The future author of Ketzot HaChoshen and Avnei Milluim became rabbi in Stryi.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 256

name: French Declaration of the Rights of Man opens the way toward Jewish emancipation
note: At the beginning of the French Revolution, the Declaration of the Rights of Man helped establish the ideological basis for Jewish civil equality in France.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: A Jew is killed at Grodno in a blood libel
note: A Jewish victim of a blood-libel accusation in Grodno.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Anti-Jewish rioters attack Warsaw
note: The Jews of Warsaw were attacked by anti-Jewish rioters in Sivan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Mobs attack Florence's Jews after civil-rights gains
note: Attacks on Jews in Florence by mobs angered by the granting of some civil rights.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: The Pale of Settlement is established in the Russian Empire
note: Catherine II's government restricted Jewish residence to western territories of the empire that became known as the Pale of Settlement.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: R. Shlomo of Karlin is killed during the Polish rebellion
note: R. Shlomo of Karlin was killed during prayer on 22 Tammuz amid the Polish rebellion.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: R. Asher of Stolin succeeds the Karlin leadership
note: After R. Shlomo of Karlin's death, R. Asher, son of R. Aharon, settled in Stolin and continued the Karlin tradition.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Fifty Jews of Ifrane choose death rather than forced conversion
note: Fifty Jews burned alive on 17 Tishrei after refusing conversion to Islam; the remainder of the Jewish community left the city.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Remaining Jews leave Ifrane after the forced-conversion crisis
note: After the deaths of those who refused conversion, the rest of the Jewish community left Ifrane.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Jews suffer under the French Reign of Terror
note: A number of Jews were among the mass arrests during the Reign of Terror despite the broader emancipation process.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Strasbourg's Jewish books are confiscated for burning
note: Confiscation of Jewish books in Strasbourg during the revolutionary period.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: The Metz yeshiva is closed during the French Revolution
note: The yeshiva in Metz was closed during the revolutionary upheaval.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Polish uprising causes Jewish casualties
note: Polish uprising causes Jewish casualties.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Yosef Shmuel Zbitkower uses funds and political influence to rescue Jews from fighting
note: The wealthy contractor Yosef Shmuel Zbitkower spent large sums and used his connections to rescue Jews endangered by the fighting.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Rioters kill Jews in Vilna after the Polish rebellion
note: Jewish deaths in Vilna in post-rebellion rioting.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Rioters kill many Jews in Warsaw after the Polish rebellion
note: A similar episode of anti-Jewish violence in Warsaw.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: The Vilna Gaon dies
note: R. Eliyahu, the Vilna Gaon, died on 19 Tishrei. His recorded teachings and annotations were published by disciples after his death.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: R. Nachum of Chernobyl dies
note: R. Menachem Nachum of Chernobyl died on 11 Cheshvan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: R. Mordechai of Chernobyl succeeds his father as rebbe
note: The twenty-eight-year-old R. Mordechai Twersky succeeded R. Nachum as leader of the Chernobyl Hasidic community.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Napoleonic occupation improves legal conditions for Jews in parts of Italy
note: Generally improved conditions for Jews in areas of Italy occupied by Napoleon's armies.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Anti-Jewish rioters attack the Jews of Ancona
note: This locality among the anti-Jewish attacks associated with the upheavals of Napoleonic Italy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Anti-Jewish rioters attack Rome's Jews before French occupation
note: This locality among the anti-Jewish attacks associated with the upheavals of Napoleonic Italy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Anti-Jewish rioters attack the Jews of Siena
note: This locality among the anti-Jewish attacks associated with the upheavals of Napoleonic Italy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 257

name: Jews are attacked and killed at Pesaro after the French withdrawal
note: This locality among the anti-Jewish attacks associated with the upheavals of Napoleonic Italy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 258

name: The Jews of Senigallia are attacked
note: This locality among the anti-Jewish attacks associated with the upheavals of Napoleonic Italy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 258

name: R. Shneur Zalman is arrested in Saint Petersburg after denunciations by opponents
note: Russian authorities arrested Shneur Zalman after accusations including treason connected with money sent to Jews in Ottoman Palestine.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 258

name: R. Shneur Zalman is released on 19 Kislev after fifty-three days
note: Shneur Zalman was cleared and released on 19 Kislev after fifty-three days in custody, a date later celebrated in Chabad tradition.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 258

name: R. Nachman of Bratslav makes a pilgrimage to Eretz Yisrael
note: Retrospectively that R. Nachman visited Eretz Yisrael in 1798 and spent Rosh Hashanah in Haifa.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: Napoleon's army advances through Eretz Yisrael to Acre
note: After campaigning in Egypt, Napoleon advanced through Eretz Yisrael as far as Acre, where his forces were halted before retreating.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 258

name: Reports circulate that Napoleon promised Jewish restoration in Eretz Yisrael
note: A report circulating in Europe that Napoleon had issued a proclamation promising a Jewish return to the land.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 258

name: R. Shneur Zalman is summoned and imprisoned a second time
note: Renewed denunciations led to Shneur Zalman's second arrest/investigation in the Russian capital.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 258

name: R. Shneur Zalman receives full freedom and settles in Liady
note: After final clearance by the new government of Alexander I, Shneur Zalman chose to establish his court at Liady.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 258

name: Blood-libel riots kill 128 Jews in Bucharest
note: 128 Jewish deaths in Bucharest after a blood-libel accusation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 258

name: Russian edict restricts Jews from villages and alcohol trade
note: The Russian government prohibited Jews from living in villages and restricted alcohol sales to peasants, creating a major displacement threat.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 258

name: Village expulsions create pressure for large-scale Jewish resettlement
note: The village-residence rules as a major expulsion measure because so many Jews lived in shtetlach and villages, though enforcement was incomplete.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 258

name: The Dubno Maggid dies
note: R. Yaakov Kranz, famed for his parables and sermons, died on 17 Tevet.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: Naftali Busnach is assassinated in Algiers
note: The wealthy Jewish political leader Naftali Busnach was assassinated by dissatisfied Ottoman soldiers.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: Jewish community of Algiers is massacred after Busnach's assassination
note: Between 200 and 500 Jews killed in the ensuing attack.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: David Bakri succeeds as head of the Algiers Jewish community
note: David Bakri, Busnach's relative and business partner, became head of the community.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: The Chida dies in Livorno
note: R. Chaim Yosef David Azulai, author of Birkei Yosef, Machazik Berachah and Shem HaGedolim, died in Livorno on 11 Adar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: Chasam Sofer becomes rabbi of Pressburg
note: R. Moshe Sofer became rabbi of Pressburg, one of the most important Jewish communities in Hungary.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: Chasam Sofer establishes the Pressburg yeshiva as a major Torah centre
note: His Pressburg rabbinate is associated with the development of a famous yeshiva and his later leadership against religious reform.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: Napoleon convenes the French 'Sanhedrin'
note: Napoleon assembled Jewish religious leaders to approve regulations previously accepted by a lay assembly, in the context of emancipation and integration.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: British bombardment of Copenhagen kills Jewish residents
note: Jewish casualties during the British bombardment of Copenhagen.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: Machatzit HaShekel is published
note: Publication of Machatzit HaShekel on Orach Chayim and says some report that its author R. Shmuel Kelin died the same year.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: Yismach Moshe becomes rabbi and rebbe in Sátoraljaújhely
note: R. Moshe Teitelbaum, disciple of the Chozeh of Lublin, became rabbi and Hasidic leader in Uhel/Sátoraljaújhely.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: Chavat Daat becomes rabbi of Leszno
note: R. Yaakov Lorberbaum, author of Chavat Daat and later Netivot HaMishpat, became rabbi of Leszno.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: R. Menachem Mendel of Shklov arrives in Safed with disciples of the Vilna Gaon
note: A group led by the Vilna Gaon's disciple R. Menachem Mendel of Shklov arrived to settle in Safed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: R. Yisrael of Shklov emigrates to Eretz Yisrael
note: Another disciple of the Vilna Gaon, R. Yisrael of Shklov, emigrated and later wrote Pe'at HaShulchan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: R. Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev dies
note: The Berditchever, a leading disciple of the Maggid and author of Kedushat Levi, died on 25 Tishrei.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: R. Avraham of Kalisk dies
note: R. Avraham of Kalisk, disciple of the Maggid and participant in the 1777 Hasidic aliyah, died on 4 Shevat.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 259

name: Chayei Adam is published
note: R. Avraham Danziger published Chayei Adam, a practical presentation of Orach Chayim law for lay readers.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: Israel Jacobson introduces an organ into Jewish worship at Seesen
note: Jacobson's 1810 service, with German hymns and organ accompaniment, is identified as an early landmark of Reform practice.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: The Reform movement begins taking institutional shape in western Germany
note: Post-Napoleonic emancipation is associated with the emergence of organized religious reform and congregational division.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: R. Nachman of Bratslav dies in Uman
note: R. Nachman, great-grandson of the Baal Shem Tov and founder of Bratslav Hasidism, died during Sukkot. His followers did not appoint a successor rebbe.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: David Bakri is beheaded by the Algerian government
note: David Bakri, head of the Algiers Jewish community, was executed by the government.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: David Duran becomes community head in Algiers and is killed the same year
note: David Duran, from a rival leading family, briefly replaced Bakri and was also killed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: Joseph Bakri becomes head of the Algiers Jewish community
note: Joseph Bakri became head of the community after the deaths of David Bakri and David Duran.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: The Shpoler Zeide dies
note: R. Aryeh Leib, the Shpoler Zeide, a popular Hasidic leader associated with warmth and emotional piety, died on 6 Tishrei.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: R. Baruch of Medzhybizh dies
note: The Baal Shem Tov's grandson R. Baruch of Medzhybizh, who had a large following and claimed broad Hasidic leadership, died on 18 Kislev.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: Greek revolutionaries attack Jews and burn synagogues in Galați
note: An attack on Jews in Galați with several synagogues burned.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: Napoleon's invasion of Eastern Europe divides Hasidic leaders
note: Different Hasidic leaders interpreted Napoleon's campaign in sharply different religious and political terms.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: R. Shneur Zalman supports the Russian war effort against Napoleon
note: Shneur Zalman's conviction that a Napoleonic victory would harm Jewish religious life and says he assisted the Russian effort.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: R. Shneur Zalman flees Liady before Napoleon's advance
note: As Napoleon's army approached, Shneur Zalman left Liady and spent months travelling with his entourage.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: R. Shneur Zalman dies during flight from Napoleon
note: His death on 24 Tevet while travelling in a small village after Napoleon's retreat.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: R. Dov Ber succeeds Shneur Zalman and settles in Lubavitch
note: Shneur Zalman's son R. Dov Ber became the next Chabad leader and established his centre in Lubavitch.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: R. Akiva Eger becomes rabbi of Poznań
note: R. Akiva Eger became rabbi of Poznań despite opposition from local maskilim.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 260

name: The Kozhnitzer Maggid dies
note: R. Yisrael, the Maggid of Kozhnitz, one of the major transmitters of Hasidism into Poland, died on 14 Tishrei.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 261

name: The Yehudi of Przysucha dies
note: R. Yaakov Yitzchak, the Yehudi HaKadosh of Przysucha, died on 19 Tishrei after developing a more introspective and demanding Hasidic style.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 261

name: R. Simcha Bunim becomes the main successor of the Yehudi of Przysucha
note: R. Simcha Bunim became the principal successor to the Yehudi and continued the Przysucha school.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 261

name: R. Menachem Mendel of Rymanów dies
note: The influential disciple of R. Elimelech of Lizhensk died on 19 Iyar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 261

name: The Chozeh of Lublin dies
note: R. Yaakov Yitzchak Horowitz, the Chozeh of Lublin, one of the leading rebbes of Poland and Galicia, died on Tisha B'Av.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 261

name: R. Yitzchak Albuker and seven Jewish leaders are killed in Algiers
note: Internal communal rivalry spilled into wider violence, killing the rabbi of Algiers and seven other Jewish leaders.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 261

name: Germany's first congregation founded explicitly on a Reform basis opens in Hamburg
note: A Reform congregation opened in Hamburg despite vehement rabbinic opposition.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 261

name: Hamburg Reform congregation prints an ideologically altered prayer book
note: The new congregation printed a prayer book with significant ideological changes a year after opening.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 261

name: Hep-Hep riots begin at Würzburg
note: An anti-Jewish riot broke out in Würzburg with the cry 'Hep! Hep!' and quickly became a wider wave.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 261

name: Hep-Hep anti-Jewish riots spread across German towns
note: Rapid spread of the riots through many German communities.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 261

name: R. Shlomo Kluger becomes rabbi in Brody
note: R. Shlomo Kluger became rabbi in Brody, where he remained for decades.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: Austria requires rabbis to study philosophy and preach in the local language
note: New regulations required rabbis to study philosophy and preach in the vernacular.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: Austria requires Jewish children to attend Christian schools
note: A law requiring Jewish children to attend Christian/general schools, part of a wider assimilationist program.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: R. Chaim of Volozhin dies
note: The disciple of the Vilna Gaon and founder of the influential Volozhin yeshiva died in Sivan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: R. Shlomo Zalman Lifshitz becomes rabbi of Warsaw
note: The author of Chemdat Shlomo became rabbi of Warsaw.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: Greek revolutionary forces kill hundreds of Jews in Iași
note: Hundreds of Jews killed in Jassy/Iași during the Greek revolt against Ottoman rule.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: Large numbers of Jews are killed in the Greek revolt
note: Some sources placed Jewish deaths in Greece during the revolt as high as 5,000.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: Anti-Jewish riots strike Odesa
note: Anti-Jewish riots in Odesa.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: Chavat Daat leaves the Leszno rabbinate over conflict with reformers
note: R. Yaakov Lorberbaum left Leszno because of a rift with a large part of the community over his strong opposition to reform.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: Expulsion of Jews from Russian villages is resumed
note: The Russian government resumed efforts to remove Jews from villages within the western empire.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: Turkish troops kill sixty Jews in Bucharest on Purim
note: Sixty Jewish deaths in Bucharest during Ottoman suppression of the Greek revolt.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: Fire destroys the Jewish quarter of Šafov
note: The Jewish section of Šafov in Moravia was destroyed by fire on 24 Sivan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: R. Klonymos Kalman Epstein of Kraków dies
note: The author of Maor VaShemesh, disciple of R. Elimelech and the Chozeh, died on 1 Tammuz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: Charleston Jews establish the first Reform group in the United States
note: A group seceded from the existing congregation after proposed reforms were rejected and created the first U.S. Reform association/congregational nucleus.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: Jews are expelled from villages around Mogilev
note: Russian authorities ordered Jews out of villages around Mogilev and into towns and cities.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: Jews are expelled from villages around Vitebsk
note: Russian authorities ordered Jews out of villages around Vitebsk.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: The Apta Rav declares a fast in response to the village-expulsion decree
note: R. Avraham Yehoshua Heshel of Apta declared a fast when the expulsion order reached Jewish communities.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: The Apta Rav dies in Medzhybizh
note: R. Avraham Yehoshua Heshel, regarded as an elder leader of Polish-Galician Hasidism, died on 5 Nisan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: R. Dov Ber of Lubavitch visits R. Akiva Eger in Poznań
note: The Chabad leader visiting R. Akiva Eger while passing through Poznań.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 262

name: R. Dov Ber of Lubavitch is exonerated after denunciation to the Russian government
note: The second Chabad rebbe was detained for questioning and completely exonerated on 10 Kislev 5587/1826.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 263

name: R. Naftali Tzvi of Ropczyce dies
note: The major Galician Hasidic leader and disciple of R. Elimelech, the Chozeh, Kozhnitz Maggid and R. Mendel of Rymanov died on 11 Iyar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 263

name: R. Meir of Apta dies
note: R. Meir of Apta, a leading disciple of the Chozeh of Lublin, died on 25 Tammuz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 263

name: Fire kills many Jews in Iași's Jewish quarter
note: Many Jewish deaths in a major fire in the Jewish section of Iași.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 263

name: Moses Montefiore makes his first visit to Eretz Yisrael
note: Moses Montefiore makes his first visit to Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 263

name: R. Simcha Bunim of Przysucha dies and R. Mendel of Kotzk becomes a principal successor
note: R. Simcha Bunim died on 12 Elul; R. Mendel of Kotzk became one of the principal heirs to the Przysucha school.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 263

name: Nicholas I orders military conscription of Jewish boys and young men
note: Nicholas I orders military conscription of Jewish boys and young men.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 263

name: Cantonist system exposes Jewish children to pressure to convert
note: Underage conscripts were placed in military cantonments and subjected to intense pressure, including violence, to accept Christianity.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 263

name: R. Dov Ber of Lubavitch dies
note: The second Chabad rebbe died on 9 Kislev, one day short of a year after the date of his exoneration.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 263

name: R. Ephraim Zalman Margolis dies
note: R. Ephraim Zalman Margolis, author of Beit Ephraim, Yad Ephraim and Matteh Ephraim, died.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Tzemach Tzedek becomes the third Chabad rebbe
note: R. Menachem Mendel, the Tzemach Tzedek, succeeded R. Dov Ber about eighteen months after his death.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 263

name: Jews are ordered to leave Kyiv
note: An expulsion order against Jews in Kyiv, though enforcement was not immediate.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Jews are ordered to leave Mykolaiv
note: A later 1829 expulsion order against Jews in the Russian port city of Nikolayev/Mykolaiv.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Jews are ordered to leave Sevastopol
note: A later 1829 expulsion order against Jews in Sevastopol.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Divrei Chaim becomes rabbi and rebbe of Tzanz
note: R. Chaim Halberstam was appointed rabbi of Tzanz/Nowy Sącz, where he built a major Hasidic following.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Reform-controlled communal leadership closes the Fürth yeshiva
note: Reform adherents gained control of the communal administration, closed R. Avraham Binyamin Wolf Hamburg's yeshiva and expelled more than one hundred students with police assistance.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Russian soldiers cause a fire that kills many Jews in Ashmyany
note: Many Jewish deaths at Oshmyany during unrest following a Polish rebellion.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: R. Moshe Mintz dies in Óbuda
note: The respected rabbi R. Moshe Mintz died in Elul in Old Buda.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Jews are expelled from Trakai after Karaite lobbying
note: The Karaites succeeded in having Jews expelled from Troki/Trakai, perhaps beginning in 1835.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: R. Tzvi Hirsch Kalischer is reported to propose buying land in Eretz Yisrael to Mayer Amschel Rothschild
note: A tradition that Kalischer proposed purchasing land in Eretz Yisrael from the Ottoman Sultan as a step toward redemption.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: R. Yisrael Lipshutz becomes rabbi of Danzig
note: The author of Tiferet Yisrael on the Mishnah became rabbi in Danzig, where he remained.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: R. Mordechai of Chernobyl dies
note: The Chernobyler Maggid died on 20 Iyar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Eight sons of R. Mordechai of Chernobyl establish successor courts
note: Succession by eight sons, each in his own locality, helping expand the Chernobyl dynastic network.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Safed earthquake kills about four thousand Jews
note: About 4,000 Jewish deaths at Safed in the Galilee earthquake of 24 Tevet.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Tiberias earthquake kills hundreds of Jews
note: Roughly 700–1,000 Jewish deaths at Tiberias in the same earthquake.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Chabad survivors of the Galilee earthquake strengthen the Hebron community
note: Some Chabad survivors moved to Hebron and joined a Chabad settlement established there about a decade earlier.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Hurva synagogue is reopened in Jerusalem after reconstruction
note: The ruined Ashkenazi synagogue associated with R. Yehuda Chasid was reopened after reconstruction.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: R. David Luria is released after forged evidence is exposed
note: R. David Luria, rabbi of Bykhaw and opponent of local maskilim and reformers, was released after denunciatory evidence was found to be forged.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Russian authorities arrest and torture hundreds of Jews in the informers affair
note: Authorities accused Jews of involvement in killings of informers and illegal exploitation; hundreds were arrested and tortured, with many dying from hard-labor sentences.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Chasam Sofer dies in Pressburg
note: R. Moshe Sofer died and was succeeded as rabbi of Pressburg by his eldest son, the Ktav Sofer.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Ktav Sofer succeeds his father as rabbi of Pressburg
note: R. Avraham Shmuel Binyamin Sofer succeeded the Chasam Sofer.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: Mashhad Jews are attacked and forced to convert to Islam
note: Many Jews were killed in an anti-Jewish attack at Mashhad; survivors were forced to convert to Islam while many secretly maintained Judaism.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 264

name: R. Yisrael of Ruzhin is released from Russian imprisonment
note: The Ruzhiner Rebbe was released after almost two years in prison on accusations connected with political ambitions and the informers affair.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 265

name: R. Yisrael of Ruzhin leaves Russia and establishes his court at Sadigura
note: After release but continued surveillance, R. Yisrael of Ruzhin left Russia and settled at Sadigura in Austrian Bukovina.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 265

name: Damascus blood libel leads to arrests and torture
note: The Damascus Affair led to arrests of Jewish adults and children, torture, deaths under interrogation and international diplomatic intervention.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 265

name: Jewish leaders are arrested on Rhodes during the wider blood-libel crisis
note: In parallel with the Damascus Affair, the rabbi and leading Jews of Rhodes were arrested.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 265

name: International Jewish delegation led by Montefiore helps secure release of Damascus prisoners
note: An international delegation of Jewish notables, including Sir Moses Montefiore, negotiated for the release of the accused Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 265

name: R. Avraham David of Buchach dies
note: R. Avraham David of Buchach, disciple of R. Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev and author of Daat Kedoshim, died on Erev Rosh Chodesh Cheshvan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 265

name: Bnei Yissachar dies
note: R. Tzvi Elimelech of Dynov, author of Bnei Yissachar and disciple of major Polish-Galician Hasidic leaders, died on 18 Tevet.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 265

name: Yismach Moshe dies in Sátoraljaújhely
note: R. Moshe Teitelbaum died on 28 Tammuz in Uhel/Sátoraljaújhely.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 265

name: R. Elazar Nisan and R. Yekutiel Yehuda continue the Yismach Moshe succession
note: Succession through Yismach Moshe's son R. Elazar Nisan and grandson R. Yekutiel Yehuda, who served in Uhel before later conflict with opponents.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 265

name: Fire in Izmir destroys manuscripts of R. Chaim Palagi
note: Destruction of some manuscripts of R. Chaim Palagi in an Izmir fire, while many of his works survived.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 265

name: Russian government convenes a commission on Jewish education and communal policy
note: A Russian government commission brought together the Tzemach Tzedek representing Chasidim, R. Yitzchak Volozhiner representing Mitnagdim, a businessman and a maskilic representative to discuss Jewish education and communal affairs.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: Tzemach Tzedek is repeatedly detained during the Russian Jewish commission
note: The Tzemach Tzedek being detained twenty-two times during the conference because of his outspoken opposition to government proposals.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: Russia repeals its ban on publication and importation of some Kabbalah and Chasidut books
note: The commission period brought repeal of an 1836 ban affecting publication and importation of certain Jewish religious books, especially Kabbalah and Chasidut.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: Russia suspends further expulsions of Jews from villages
note: Suspension of the ongoing program of removing Jews from shtetlach and villages.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: Russia orders state schools for Jewish children
note: Nicholas I's government ordered state schools for Jewish children following Max Lilienthal's educational lobbying.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: Russia orders government-style rabbinical seminaries
note: The government directed the creation of rabbinical seminaries with secular education, intended to train state-recognized rabbis.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: Russian authorities weaken the traditional Jewish communal structure
note: Abolition or weakening of the older communal framework and introduction of government-appointed rabbis, substantially reducing traditional communal autonomy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: Max Lilienthal leaves Russia and settles in the United States
note: After becoming politically controversial in Russia, Max Lilienthal left for the United States, where he became active in the Reform movement alongside Isaac Mayer Wise.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: Sir Moses Montefiore visits Russia to intercede for the Jews
note: Montefiore travelled to Russia seeking relief from discriminatory decrees and met Jewish leaders and government officials.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: Cholera epidemic kills many Jews in Vilna
note: Many Jewish deaths during the 1848 cholera epidemic in Vilna.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: R. Yisrael Salanter publicly eats on Yom Kippur during the cholera emergency
note: Following medical advice during the epidemic, R. Yisrael Salanter publicly ate in synagogue as an example to protect health.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: R. Yisrael Salanter refuses leadership of the government rabbinical seminary
note: He declined an invitation to head the government-sponsored rabbinical seminary despite encouragement from R. Yitzchak Volozhiner.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: R. Yisrael Salanter leaves Vilna and settles in Kovno
note: After refusing the seminary position, R. Yisrael Salanter was compelled to leave Vilna and settled in Kovno for about nine years.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: R. Meir of Premishlan dies
note: R. Meir of Premishlan dies.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 266

name: R. Shimshon Raphael Hirsch becomes rabbi of Frankfurt
note: Hirsch became rabbi in Frankfurt and developed an Orthodox communal model combining full halachic commitment with engagement with contemporary culture.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: Hirsch establishes schools combining traditional Jewish and secular studies
note: The development of Jewish schools in Hirsch's community that retained traditional education while including secular studies.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: German Orthodox communal consolidation develops around Hirsch's Frankfurt model
note: Hirsch's congregational model strengthened halacha-observant Judaism in a German environment shaped by Reform, Haskalah and assimilation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: Nicholas I increases Jewish military-conscription quotas during the Crimean War
note: The Russian government increased quotas of Jewish conscripts and cantonists as the Crimean War began.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: Russia restricts Jewish styles of dress
note: New imperial decrees restricting traditional Jewish clothing.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: Russian law classifies Jews into discriminatory economic categories
note: Jews were placed into economic classes carrying different legal restrictions and residence rights.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: Orthodox Jews in Mainz form a separate congregation after installation of an organ
note: A group broke away from the synagogue after an organ was installed and established its own Orthodox congregation under Rabbi Marcus Lehmann.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: R. Shalom of Belz dies
note: R. Shalom of Belz, disciple of the Chozeh of Lublin and the Apta Rav, died on 27 Elul.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: R. Yehoshua of Belz succeeds his father as rebbe
note: R. Yehoshua succeeded R. Shalom as the Hasidic leader of Belz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: Pitchei Teshuva leaves Grodno for the rabbinate of Utena
note: R. Avraham Tzvi Hirsch Eisenstadt, author of Pitchei Teshuva, left Grodno to become rabbi in Utena.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: R. Yosef Shaul Nathanson becomes rabbi of Lviv
note: The author of Sho'el UMeshiv became rabbi of Lviv and was active against maskilic educational reform.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: Machine-baked matzah becomes the subject of a major halachic controversy
note: R. Yosef Shaul Nathanson permitted machine-made matzah, helping trigger a broad halachic controversy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: R. Yisrael Salanter moves west and lectures to Jewish university students in Germany
note: Salanter travelled to Germany for health reasons and attracted Jewish university students to Torah and Mussar lectures delivered in German.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: R. Yisrael Salanter later settles in Memel
note: After his German period, Salanter settled in Memel on the Lithuanian-German border.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: A Jewish man in Tunisia is killed after an accusation of insulting Islam
note: A mob attack followed by the killing of a Jew in Tunisia on an allegation of insulting Islam.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: Yetev Lev becomes rabbi and rebbe of Sighet
note: R. Yekutiel Yehuda Teitelbaum became rabbi of Sighet and Hasidic rebbe.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 267

name: The Malbim becomes rabbi of Bucharest
note: The biblical commentator Malbim became rabbi in Bucharest, where he encountered strong opposition from Reform-oriented groups.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: Edgardo Mortara is seized from his Jewish family in Bologna
note: Church authorities removed six-year-old Edgardo Mortara from his parents after a claimed secret baptism and raised him as a Christian despite an international campaign for his return.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: R. Menachem Mendel of Kotzk dies
note: The Kotzker Rebbe died on 22 Shevat after a long period of seclusion.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: Chidushei HaRim becomes a principal successor to the Kotzker school
note: R. Yitzchak Meir Alter, later based in Ger, became the principal continuation of the Kotzker tradition.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: Anti-Jewish rioters kill Jews in Galați
note: Many Jewish deaths in an attack at Galați.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: Jews are attacked in Odesa
note: An anti-Jewish attack in nearby Odesa in the same period.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: Jews of Tétouan are massacred
note: A massacre of the Jewish community of Tétouan during conflict involving Spain and Morocco.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: Moroccan Jews flee toward Gibraltar and Eretz Yisrael
note: Violence and war caused Jewish flight from Moroccan communities; some refugees reached Gibraltar and some later settled in Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: Alliance Israélite Universelle is founded
note: The Alliance Israélite Universelle was established to aid Jews facing persecution and poverty through diplomacy, migration assistance and education.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: Maharam Schick becomes rabbi of Khust
note: R. Moshe Schick became rabbi in Khust and developed it into a major Orthodox centre in northern Hungary.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: R. Yisrael Zev Horowitz dies in Tiberias
note: The Chasam Sofer's disciple R. Yisrael Zev Horowitz died in Tiberias after settling in Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: General Grant orders Jews expelled from his military department
note: During the American Civil War, General Ulysses S. Grant issued an order expelling Jews from his military department, including parts of Tennessee.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: President Lincoln orders Grant's anti-Jewish expulsion revoked
note: President Lincoln instructed Grant to revoke the order only weeks later.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 268

name: The Malbim is imprisoned in Bucharest after denunciation
note: Assimilationist and Reform opponents denounced the Malbim; he was arrested and later released after intervention by Moses Montefiore.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: The Malbim is expelled from Romania
note: The Malbim's release was conditioned on leaving Romania.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: Jewish communities in Tunis and Tripoli are massacred on Yom Kippur
note: Massacres of Jews in several North African cities, including Tunis and Tripoli, by insurgent tribes.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: Chidushei HaRim dies
note: R. Yitzchak Meir Alter of Ger died on 23 Adar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: Tiferet Shlomo of Radomsk dies
note: R. Shlomo HaKohen of Radomsk died on Erev Rosh Chodesh Nisan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: Tzemach Tzedek of Lubavitch dies
note: R. Menachem Mendel Schneersohn, the Tzemach Tzedek, died on 13 Nisan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: R. Shmuel succeeds the Tzemach Tzedek in Lubavitch
note: The Tzemach Tzedek's youngest son R. Shmuel became the central Lubavitch successor, while several brothers established courts elsewhere.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: Romania expels Jews from numerous villages
note: Broad expulsions of Jews from Romanian villages and discriminatory harassment of those who remained.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: Jewish refugees drown in the Danube while fleeing Romanian expulsions
note: Some Jewish refugees drowning in the Danube during the expulsions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: Montefiore visits Romania to seek repeal of anti-Jewish measures
note: Sir Moses Montefiore made a personal visit in an attempt to have discriminatory measures repealed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: Hungarian Orthodox communities separate from the central Jewish communal structure
note: After Jewish emancipation in Hungary, Orthodox representatives established a separate communal organization when Neolog leaders rejected subordination of communal rules to the Shulchan Aruch.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: Ktav Sofer and Maharam Schick help organize separate Hungarian Orthodoxy
note: The Ktav Sofer and Maharam Schick as major organizers of the new Orthodox communal structure.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: R. Azriel Hildesheimer leaves Eisenstadt for Berlin
note: Hildesheimer, who disagreed with separate Orthodoxy in Hungary, moved to Berlin and developed an Orthodox approach related to Hirsch's model.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: Ben Ish Chai visits Eretz Yisrael
note: R. Yosef Chaim of Baghdad, later widely known through Ben Ish Chai, visited Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: R. Raphael Meir Panigel reports seeing alleged Temple vessels in Rome
note: Panigel's report that the Pope showed him objects said to have been taken from the Beit HaMikdash by the Romans.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: Anti-Jewish riots strike Odesa during Pesach
note: Anti-Jewish riots in Odesa during Pesach.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: R. Shmuel Strashun (Rashash) dies in Vilna
note: R. Shmuel Strashun, author of Hagahot HaRashash on the Talmud, died in Vilna.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: Chafetz Chaim is published anonymously
note: R. Yisrael Meir Kagan anonymously published Chafetz Chaim, his influential halachic work on forbidden speech.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 269

name: R. Yitzchak Yehuda Yechiel of Komarno dies
note: The Komarno rebbe and prolific kabbalistic writer died on 10 Iyar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 270

name: Minchat Chinuch dies
note: R. Yosef Babad, author of Minchat Chinuch, died in 1874.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 270

name: Aruch HaShulchan becomes rabbi of Novogrudok
note: R. Yechiel Michel Epstein became rabbi in Novogrudok, where he later produced Aruch HaShulchan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 270

name: Divrei Chaim of Tzanz dies
note: R. Chaim Halberstam of Tzanz died on 25 Nisan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 270

name: The Tzanz dynasty branches among the Divrei Chaim's sons and grandson
note: Succession by six sons, including the Divrei Yechezkel of Shineva, and by grandson R. Shlomo of Bobov.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 270

name: Petah Tikva is founded as an agricultural Jewish settlement
note: Halacha-observant Jews from Jerusalem and immigrants from Hungary established Petah Tikva, an early agricultural settlement aimed at economic self-reliance.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 270

name: Machazikei Hadat is founded to organize Orthodox political action
note: R. Shimon Sofer and R. Yehoshua of Belz founded Machazikei Hadat to counter organized maskilic influence and contest parliamentary elections.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 270

name: R. Yaakov Abuhatzeira dies in Egypt on his way to Eretz Yisrael
note: The Moroccan kabbalist R. Yaakov Abuhatzeira died in Egypt on 20 Tevet while travelling toward Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 270

name: Pogrom wave begins across the Russian Empire
note: After the assassination of Alexander II, anti-Jewish violence spread across southern and western parts of the Russian Empire and continued sporadically for several years.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 270

name: Mass Jewish emigration from Eastern Europe accelerates
note: A huge migration wave beginning in the 1880s, primarily toward the United States, with smaller movements toward Western Europe and Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: Hovevei Zion groups form in response to Russian conditions
note: Small groups began organizing around Jewish settlement in Eretz Yisrael, helping create a proto-Zionist settlement movement.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: Jewish migrants increasingly choose the United States
note: The United States became the dominant destination for East European Jewish migration.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: Small Hovevei Zion groups begin emigrating to Eretz Yisrael
note: Small Hovevei Zion groups begin emigrating to Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: Government closes the Chabad yeshiva at Starodub after denunciation
note: A Chabad yeshiva in Starodub being closed by the Russian government after denunciation by a local maskil.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: Anti-Jewish riots strike Algiers and other Algerian cities
note: Recurring anti-Jewish violence in Algeria over several years, with deaths, synagogue attacks and desecrated Torah scrolls.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: Russia enacts the May Laws restricting Jewish rural settlement
note: The May Laws prohibited new Jewish settlement in many peasant villages within the Pale and imposed further economic restrictions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: Russian authorities use the May Laws to remove Jews from rural settlements
note: The laws as producing broad village expulsions, although enforcement was uneven.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: Tiszaeszlár blood libel triggers anti-Jewish agitation in Hungary
note: Jews were accused in the Tiszaeszlár blood libel; although acquitted, the case contributed to widespread anti-Jewish riots and agitation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: R. Shmuel of Lubavitch dies
note: The fourth Chabad rebbe died on 13 Tishrei.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: R. Yisrael Salanter dies
note: The founder of the modern Mussar movement died in Germany on 25 Shevat after periods in Paris and Germany.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: Yetev Lev dies in Sighet and is succeeded by R. Chananyah Yom Tov Lipa
note: R. Yekutiel Yehuda Teitelbaum died on 6 Elul and his son became rabbi and rebbe in Sighet.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: R. Shmuel Ehrenfeld dies
note: R. Shmuel Ehrenfeld, grandson of the Chasam Sofer and author of Chatan Sofer, died while serving in Mattersdorf.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 271

name: R. Menachem Mendel of Vizhnitz dies
note: The Vizhnitz rebbe and author of Tzemach Tzadik died on Erev Rosh Chodesh Cheshvan and was succeeded by his son R. Baruch.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 272

name: R. Avraham of Slonim dies
note: The Slonim rebbe, author of Yesod HaAvodah, died on 11 Cheshvan.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 272

name: Pittsburgh Platform defines a strongly Reform American religious program
note: A Reform conference adopted principles rejecting the continuing authority of traditional halachic observance in several areas.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 272

name: Reaction to radical Reform helps crystallize the American Conservative movement
note: Opposition to the Pittsburgh Platform is associated with the later development of Conservative Judaism among more traditional but non-Orthodox scholars and laypeople.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 272

name: R. Shlomo Ganzfried dies in Uzhhorod
note: R. Shlomo Ganzfried dies in Uzhhorod.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 272

name: R. Meir Simcha HaKohen becomes rabbi in Dvinsk
note: The future author of Or Sameach became a rabbi in Dvinsk, where he remained for decades.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 272

name: R. Yaakov Yosef is brought from Vilna to become chief rabbi of New York
note: A coalition of Orthodox congregations brought R. Yaakov Yosef to New York in an attempt to create centralized religious authority.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 272

name: New York has roughly 130 Orthodox synagogues
note: A snapshot of a rapidly growing but fragmented immigrant Orthodox community.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 272

name: Rogatchover Gaon becomes rabbi of the Chasidic community in Dvinsk
note: R. Yosef Rozin became rabbi of Dvinsk's Chasidic community and produced works titled Tzafnat Paneach.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 272

name: British Chief Rabbi Nathan Marcus Adler dies
note: Nathan Marcus Adler, Chief Rabbi of the British Empire, died on 29 Tevet.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 272
