name: A committee in Eretz Yisrael promotes Hebrew as an everyday spoken language
note: Establishment of a committee promoting Hebrew for daily use.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 272

name: Mass expulsion of Jews from Moscow begins
note: Mass expulsion of Jews from Moscow begins.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 272

name: R. Chaim Soloveitchik becomes rabbi of Brisk
note: After leaving Volozhin, R. Chaim Soloveitchik became rabbi in Brisk and developed the analytical method later associated with Brisker learning.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 273

name: Volozhin yeshiva is closed after Russian government pressure
note: Volozhin yeshiva is closed after Russian government pressure.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 273

name: Netziv leaves Volozhin after the yeshiva closure
note: R. Naftali Tzvi Yehuda Berlin left Volozhin after government demands concerning secular studies and student numbers contributed to closure of the yeshiva.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 273

name: Netziv dies in Warsaw
note: The Netziv died in Warsaw while hoping to settle in Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 273

name: Alfred Dreyfus is falsely convicted of espionage
note: The conviction of French Jewish army officer Alfred Dreyfus became a major public antisemitic crisis.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 273

name: The Dreyfus affair pushes Theodor Herzl toward political Zionism
note: Herzl's response to the antisemitic atmosphere surrounding Dreyfus as a major catalyst for his advocacy of a sovereign Jewish state.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 273

name: Political Zionism begins consolidating scattered return-to-Zion groups
note: Herzl began intensive political organizing that would soon bring multiple proto-Zionist groups into a formal congress movement.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 273

name: R. Yitzchak Elchanan Spektor dies in Kovno
note: The prominent rabbi of Kovno and supporter of settlement in Eretz Yisrael died in Adar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 273

name: Solomon Schechter transfers a huge Cairo Geniza collection to Cambridge
note: Schechter brought a very large collection of manuscripts from the Ben Ezra Synagogue geniza in Fustat/Cairo to Cambridge University.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 273

name: Anti-Jewish rioters attack Mostaganem
note: Anti-Jewish violence in Mostaganem, Algeria.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 273

name: The Jewish Labour Bund is founded secretly in Vilna
note: A Jewish socialist workers' union was founded in Vilna and later became a major force in Jewish socialist politics and secular Yiddish culture.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 273

name: Anti-Jewish pogrom strikes Bucharest
note: A pogrom in Bucharest in Kislev.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 273

name: Sdei Chemed returns to Jerusalem and then becomes rabbi in Hebron
note: R. Chaim Hezekiah Medini returned from decades in Crimea and Constantinople to Eretz Yisrael, declined the Sephardi chief rabbinate and became rabbi in Hebron.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Leopold Hilsner is sentenced to death in a Bohemian blood libel
note: Hilsner was condemned in a blood-libel case that generated major antisemitic publicity; the sentence was later reduced to life imprisonment.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: R. Tzadok HaKohen of Lublin dies
note: R. Tzadok HaKohen, author of Pri Tzadik and a major Hasidic thinker, died on 9 Elul.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Jewish population of Eretz Yisrael reaches roughly fifty thousand
note: An approximate Jewish population of 50,000 in Eretz Yisrael at this stage.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Jewish population of the United States reaches roughly one million
note: An approximate U.S. Jewish population of one million.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Kishinev pogrom kills forty-nine Jews
note: Kishinev pogrom kills forty-nine Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Gomel pogrom kills eight Jews
note: Eight Jewish deaths at Gomel and notes that Jewish self-defenders were themselves prosecuted.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Marcus Jastrow dies in the United States
note: Marcus Jastrow, author of the influential Aramaic-English dictionary, died in Tishrei.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: R. Chananyah Yom Tov Lipa Teitelbaum dies
note: The Sighet rebbe died in Shevat.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: R. Chaim Tzvi and R. Yoel Teitelbaum emerge as successor figures
note: Succession through R. Chaim Tzvi in Sighet and the later rise of R. Yoel Teitelbaum, who would become the Satmar rebbe.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: R. Yaakov Chaim Sofer settles in Eretz Yisrael
note: The Baghdad scholar who authored Kaf HaChaim settled in Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Sfas Emes dies and is succeeded by R. Avraham Mordechai Alter
note: R. Yehuda Aryeh Leib Alter of Ger died on 5 Shevat and was succeeded by his son.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: State-tolerated pogrom wave sweeps the Russian Empire
note: Almost 700 pogroms over less than two years and more than 800 Jewish deaths amid revolutionary unrest and official antisemitic incitement.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Zhytomyr pogrom kills twenty-five Jews
note: Approximately 25 Jewish deaths in this locality during the 1905 pogrom wave.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Yekaterinoslav pogrom kills about one hundred twenty Jews
note: Approximately 120 Jewish deaths in this locality during the 1905 pogrom wave.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Simferopol pogrom kills about forty Jews
note: Approximately 40 Jewish deaths in this locality during the 1905 pogrom wave.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Rechytsa pogrom kills about fifty Jews
note: Approximately 50 Jewish deaths in this locality during the 1905 pogrom wave.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Odesa pogrom kills about three hundred Jews
note: Approximately 300 Jewish deaths in this locality during the 1905 pogrom wave.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 274

name: Białystok pogrom kills about seventy Jews
note: 70 Jews killed and 70 seriously injured in the Białystok pogrom.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: Siedlce pogrom kills about thirty Jews
note: 30 Jewish deaths at Siedlce.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: R. Yosef Engel becomes rabbi in Kraków
note: The prolific halachic and kabbalistic scholar R. Yosef Engel became rabbi in Kraków.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: Casablanca riots kill thirty Jews and abduct women and children
note: 30 Jewish deaths and the abduction of 250 women and children in tribal violence in Casablanca.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: Another Kishinev pogrom kills nineteen Jews
note: 19 Jewish deaths in a later Kishinev pogrom.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: R. Shmuel Salant dies in Jerusalem
note: The long-serving Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Jerusalem died in Av after decades in the city.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: R. Chaim Berlin succeeds R. Shmuel Salant
note: R. Chaim Berlin succeeding him in Jerusalem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: Jerusalem's Jewish community is described as growing from about 500 to about 30,000 since 1841
note: Jerusalem's Jewish community is described as growing from about 500 to about 30,000 since 1841.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: Tel Aviv is founded as a suburb of Jaffa
note: The founding of Tel Aviv as a new Jewish suburb of Jaffa.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: R. Avraham Bornsztain of Sochaczew dies
note: The Sochatchover rebbe, author of Avnei Nezer and Eglei Tal, died on 11 Adar I.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: First volume of Chazon Ish is published anonymously
note: R. Avraham Yeshaya Karelitz anonymously published the first volume of Chazon Ish.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: Menahem Mendel Beilis is arrested in the Kiev blood libel
note: Beilis was imprisoned on extremely weak evidence in a ritual-murder accusation that drew international attention.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: Agudat Yisrael is founded at Katowice
note: An international Orthodox political organization was established to strengthen adherence to Halacha amid Reform, assimilationist, socialist and secular nationalist pressures.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: Beilis is acquitted after his Kiev trial
note: After two years in prison, Beilis was tried and freed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: R. Tzvi Hirsch Shapira of Munkács dies
note: The author of Darkei Teshuva died on 16 Tishrei and was succeeded by his son R. Chaim Elazar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: R. Chaim Elazar Shapira succeeds in Munkács
note: R. Chaim Elazar became the Munkács rebbe and a major polemical Orthodox leader.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: R. Yitzchak HaLevi Rabinowitz dies
note: The rabbi of Hamburg and author of Dorot HaRishonim, who helped motivate Agudat Yisrael's formation, died on 20 Iyar.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: More than half a million Jewish soldiers serve in World War I
note: More than half a million Jewish soldiers serve in World War I.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 275

name: Russia expels Jews from towns near the World War I front
note: As military defeats generated suspicion of treason and espionage, Russian authorities expelled Jews from towns near the front and deported many into the interior.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Russia prohibits printing in Hebrew characters near the front
note: The wartime prohibition also silenced Yiddish newspapers and restricted vital local information.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: German army burns part of the Jewish quarter of Kalisz
note: 33 Jewish deaths when invading German forces set fire to the Jewish section of Kalisz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Jewish population of Eretz Yisrael is about eighty-five thousand during World War I
note: 85,000 Jews living under Ottoman rule is estimated at this stage.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Wartime starvation kills thousands of Jews in Eretz Yisrael and drives others away
note: Severe wartime hunger, death and emigration from Ottoman Palestine.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: United States Jewish population reaches about 3.25 million
note: An approximate U.S. Jewish population of 3.25 million.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: American Jews raise large relief funds for war-stricken Jewish communities
note: U.S. Jews raised substantial assistance for Jews in Russia, occupied areas and Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Leo Frank is lynched in Georgia
note: Leo Frank was killed by an antisemitic mob after a murder conviction based on weak evidence.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Russian provisional government abolishes most legal restrictions on Jews
note: After the fall of Nicholas II, the provisional government removed most anti-Jewish restrictions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: The Pale of Settlement is abolished
note: The legal residence restrictions of the Pale ended during the Russian Revolution.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Bolsheviks seize power and the Russian Civil War begins
note: Bolshevik seizure of power plunged the former empire into civil war, during which Jewish communities suffered attacks from multiple armed forces.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Sarah Schenirer opens the first Bais Yaakov school in Kraków
note: A small school for traditional Jewish education of girls became the foundation of the Bais Yaakov educational movement.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Britain issues the Balfour Declaration
note: The British government announced support for establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Australian Light Horse captures Beersheba
note: British imperial forces captured Beersheba from the Ottoman Empire during the Palestine campaign.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: British forces capture Jaffa and Tel Aviv area
note: British forces captured Jaffa and Tel Aviv from the Ottoman Empire; Jews who had been expelled by Ottoman authorities returned.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: British forces capture Jerusalem
note: Jerusalem passed from Ottoman to British control during World War I.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Salonika fire leaves tens of thousands of Jews homeless
note: A major fire destroyed much of Salonika and left about 50,000 Jews homeless, contributing to later emigration.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Russian Civil War pogrom wave kills tens of thousands of Jews
note: More than 525 Jewish communities attacked over roughly two years and gives a total of over 60,000 Jewish deaths.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Ninety Jews are killed at Novhorod-Siverskyi
note: 90 Jewish deaths in an attack by retreating Red Army troops.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: R. Chaim Brisker dies
note: R. Chaim Soloveitchik died on 21 Av.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Lviv pogrom kills about seventy Jews
note: Polish soldiers fighting Ukrainians for control of eastern Galicia killed about 70 Jews in Lviv.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Proskurov pogrom kills about seventeen hundred Jews
note: About 1,700 Jewish deaths in a four-hour pogrom by Ukrainian nationalist forces.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 276

name: Zhytomyr pogroms kill Jews in multiple waves
note: 80 Jewish deaths in one attack and 317 in another during the 1919 violence.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Thirty-five Jews are executed at Pinsk
note: Polish forces executed 35 Jews on dubious allegations.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Two Jews are killed in a Kalisz pogrom
note: Two Jewish deaths in Kalisz.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Cherkasy pogroms kill hundreds of Jews
note: About 700 Jews killed by Cossacks in Iyar and a further 250 by White Russian forces in Av.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Trostianets pogrom kills about four hundred Jews
note: Approximately 400 Jewish deaths at Trostianets.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Tulchyn pogrom kills about one hundred seventy Jews
note: Approximately 170 Jewish deaths at Tulchyn.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Polish troops kill about eighty Jews in Vilna
note: About 80 Jewish deaths at Vilna during the conflict.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: White Russian forces massacre Jews at Bohuslav
note: 40 Jewish deaths at Bohuslav on 30 Av.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Petliura's forces execute Jews in Kyiv
note: 36 Jews executed in Kyiv by Ukrainian forces.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Fastiv pogrom kills about fifteen hundred Jews
note: Approximately 1,500 Jews killed by White Russian forces at Fastiv.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: R. David of Skvira dies in Kyiv after fleeing unrest
note: The Skvira rebbe moved his family to Kyiv because of pogroms and unrest and died there on 15 Kislev.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Arab attack at Tel Hai kills eight Jewish defenders including Joseph Trumpeldor
note: Arab nationalist attacks struck northern Jewish settlements; eight defenders were killed at Tel Hai.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Arab attack in Jerusalem kills five Jews during Pesach
note: Five Jewish deaths in Jerusalem during an Arab attack.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Yevsektsiya intensifies suppression of Jewish religious life in Soviet Russia
note: The Soviet Jewish Section, aided by security organs, closed synagogues and Jewish schools and persecuted rabbis, teachers and ritual functionaries.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Rashab of Lubavitch dies in Rostov
note: R. Shalom Dov Ber Schneersohn died on 2 Nisan after relocating from Lubavitch during the war.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: R. Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn succeeds as Lubavitcher Rebbe
note: The new Lubavitcher Rebbe expanded religious and relief activity across Soviet Russia.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Britain assumes formal Mandate control in Eretz Yisrael
note: Formal British control under the internationally endorsed Palestine Mandate.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: R. Avraham Yitzchak Kook becomes first Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi under the new council
note: The Jerusalem rabbinical council invited R. Kook to serve as Av Beit Din and Ashkenazi chief rabbi.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Edah HaCharedit develops as an alternative rabbinic council
note: Opponents of the Zionist-influenced chief-rabbinate structure, including R. Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld and R. Yitzchak Yerucham Diskin, established a separate council that became the Edah HaCharedit.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Tetiiv pogrom kills thousands of Jews
note: About 4,000 Jews killed by armed bands in Tetiiv.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: R. David Abuhatzeira is killed in Morocco
note: R. David Abuhatzeira killed by cannon fire.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Jaffa riots kill forty-seven Jews
note: 47 Jewish deaths in Arab riots in Jaffa.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Four Jews are killed defending Petah Tikva
note: Four Jewish defenders were killed during an Arab attack on Petah Tikva.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: R. Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz becomes rosh yeshiva in New York
note: Mendlowitz became a major force in rebuilding traditional Torah education in the United States.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 277

name: Mordecai Kaplan's daughter participates in an early American Bat Mitzvah ceremony
note: Kaplan's ceremony for his daughter is identified as an important landmark in the growing Bat Mitzvah custom, while noting claims of earlier precedents.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: Reconstructionism begins to emerge around Mordecai Kaplan
note: Kaplan moved from an Orthodox background through Conservative scholarship toward the movement later called Reconstructionism.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: Daf HaYomi study cycle begins
note: R. Meir Shapiro instituted the daily folio study cycle beginning on Rosh Hashanah 5684.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: Lubavitch builds a clandestine network of Jewish religious institutions in Soviet Russia
note: R. Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn organized teachers, shochtim, rabbis and schools to maintain Jewish religious life despite Soviet repression.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: Lubavitcher Rebbe is forced from Rostov and moves to Leningrad
note: Security pressure forced R. Yosef Yitzchak to leave Rostov and continue his underground work from Leningrad.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: Jewish population of Eretz Yisrael reaches roughly one hundred twenty thousand
note: Jewish population of Eretz Yisrael reaches roughly one hundred twenty thousand.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: Jewish population of the United States reaches roughly 4.5 million
note: Jewish population of the United States reaches roughly 4.5 million.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: R. Menachem Kasher settles in Jerusalem
note: The author of Torah Sheleimah settled in Jerusalem and became a rosh yeshiva.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: Slobodka yeshiva transfers a major branch to Hebron
note: The original Slobodka yeshiva was transferred to Eretz Yisrael and established in Hebron.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: R. Isser Zalman Meltzer settles in Jerusalem as rosh yeshiva
note: The author of Even HaEzel settled in Jerusalem and became a rosh yeshiva.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: Soviets arrest the Lubavitcher Rebbe for underground religious activity
note: R. Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested, abused and sentenced to death without trial for organizing clandestine Jewish religious life.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: Lubavitcher Rebbe is released and expelled from Soviet Russia
note: International pressure helped secure his release; he was expelled and settled in Riga while continuing to guide the Soviet underground from abroad.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: R. Yoel Teitelbaum is appointed rabbi of Satmar
note: R. Yoel Teitelbaum was appointed rabbi in Satmar amid local opposition; his supporters ultimately prevailed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: Jewish population of Eretz Yisrael reaches roughly one hundred fifty thousand
note: Jewish population of Eretz Yisrael reaches roughly one hundred fifty thousand.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 278

name: Hebron massacre kills about sixty Jews and destroys the community
note: About 60 Jewish deaths in the Hebron massacre; survivors relocated mainly to Jerusalem.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Hebron survivors move to Jerusalem
note: The destruction of the Hebron community forced surviving families to relocate.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Franz Rosenzweig dies
note: Rosenzweig died at age 43 after a major intellectual and religious return toward halachic Jewish life.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Lubavitcher Rebbe visits Eretz Yisrael and the United States
note: R. Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn travelled to Eretz Yisrael and then the United States to encourage religious observance and raise funds.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: R. Yechezkel Abramsky leaves Soviet Russia and settles in London
note: After hard labor in the Soviet Union, R. Yechezkel Abramsky was released and permitted to settle in London.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Nazis come to power in Germany
note: The Nazi Party under Adolf Hitler took power and immediately began intensifying economic, legal and physical persecution of Germany's Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Chafetz Chaim dies
note: R. Yisrael Meir Kagan, the Chafetz Chaim, died on 24 Elul.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Constantine riots kill twenty-five Jews
note: 25 Jewish deaths and many injuries in attacks at Constantine; resistance by Jews helped end the violence.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: R. Avraham Yitzchak Kook dies
note: R. Kook died on 3 Elul after serving as Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Regina Jonas is ordained as a rabbi in Germany
note: The head of the Liberal Rabbis Association in Offenbach ordaining Regina Jonas on December 25, 1935.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Arab riots in Tel Aviv kill eighteen Jews
note: 18 Jewish deaths in Tel Aviv in the opening phase of the Arab Revolt.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Arab Revolt begins against Jewish immigration and British rule
note: Arab Revolt begins against Jewish immigration and British rule.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Jewish immigration to Eretz Yisrael continues despite the Arab Revolt
note: About 60,000 Jews entered during the three years of revolt, after about 164,000 arrivals in the preceding three years.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: The re-established Hebron Jewish community ceases to exist again
note: The renewed violence ended the recently re-established Jewish community in Hebron.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Przytyk pogrom kills three Jews and wounds dozens
note: Three Jewish deaths and about 60 wounded in a pogrom at Przytyk.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Bomb attack in Timișoara kills two Jews
note: Two Jewish deaths in a bombing in Timișoara.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Anti-Jewish attacks spread across Polish cities
note: Attacks on Jews in many Polish cities during 1938.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Five-day working week in the United States makes Shabbat observance easier for many workers
note: Five-day working week in the United States makes Shabbat observance easier for many workers.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Evian Conference fails to open major refugee routes for German and Austrian Jews
note: Delegates from 32 countries met to address the refugee crisis but most states refused to loosen immigration restrictions substantially.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 279

name: Italy expels Jews of foreign origin
note: Mussolini's government ordered Jews of foreign origin expelled from Italy.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 280

name: Kristallnacht pogroms sweep Germany and Austria
note: Nazi-directed nationwide violence destroyed synagogues and Jewish businesses, led to mass arrests and marked a major escalation in persecution.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 280

name: Tens of thousands of Jewish men are arrested after Kristallnacht
note: About 30,000 arrests and deportations to concentration camps following the November pogrom.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 280

name: Synagogues and Jewish property are destroyed during Kristallnacht
note: Hundreds of synagogues and more than a thousand Jewish properties destroyed, with Torah scrolls and cemeteries desecrated.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 280

name: Germany invades Poland and begins World War II in Europe
note: Nazi Germany invaded Poland, beginning World War II in Europe and a rapid escalation of persecution and mass killing of Jews in occupied territory.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 285

name: German forces massacre several hundred Jews in Częstochowa
note: Several hundred Jews killed shortly after the German conquest of Częstochowa.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 285

name: German forces burn the Będzin synagogue and Jewish quarter
note: German forces burn the Będzin synagogue and Jewish quarter.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 285

name: Soviet Union annexes eastern Poland and Jewish refugees flee eastward
note: Following the German-Soviet partition of Poland, many Jews fled from German-occupied territory into the Soviet zone.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 285

name: Soviet authorities deport Jewish refugees and residents deeper into the USSR
note: Soviet authorities suppressed organized Jewish life and deported many people from annexed eastern Poland to labor settlements and camps in the Soviet interior. Paradoxically, some deportees thereby survived the later German occupation.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 285

name: German troops kill about five hundred Jews in Przemyśl
note: About 500 Jews killed after German forces captured Przemyśl.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 285

name: German troops kill the Jews remaining in Ostrów Mazowiecka
note: 560 Jews who had not escaped across the nearby Soviet border were killed.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 285

name: Nazis begin systematic use of Polish Jews for forced labor
note: The beginning of widespread compulsory slave labor imposed on Polish Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 285

name: Piotrków becomes one of the first Nazi ghettos in occupied Poland
note: The Jews of Piotrków were confined to a ghetto, an early step in the broader policy of concentrating Polish Jews in overcrowded urban ghettos.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 285

name: Nazi ghettoization campaign expands across occupied Poland
note: German authorities increasingly forced Jews into ghettos, including the largest centers in Warsaw, Kraków and Lublin, where crowding, hunger and disease caused enormous mortality.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 285

name: Lubavitcher Rebbe escapes occupied Europe and reaches New York
note: R. Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn escaped Warsaw via Berlin and Latvia and reached the United States, where he immediately began rebuilding Torah education.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 285

name: Lubavitch establishes new yeshiva and education network in the United States
note: Within days of arrival, R. Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn established a yeshiva and began a broad program of schools, publications and study sessions.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 285

name: Auschwitz concentration camp opens
note: Auschwitz concentration camp opens.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: German forces conquer Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands, Belgium and France
note: By mid-1940 Nazi Germany controlled much of western and northern Europe, bringing millions more Jews under direct or indirect German domination.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: Patria explodes and sinks in Haifa harbor
note: Patria explodes and sinks in Haifa harbor.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: Jewish businesses are seized in Constanța
note: Armed bands confiscated Jewish businesses while Romanian government representatives stood by; people who resisted disappeared. The port nevertheless remained an escape route from Europe.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: Chełm death march kills about fourteen hundred Jews
note: 1,800 Jews forced on a death march from Chełm, with about 1,400 shot along the way.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: Imrei Emes of Ger escapes Warsaw and reaches Eretz Yisrael
note: R. Avraham Mordechai Alter, the Imrei Emes of Ger, escaped occupied Warsaw and reached Eretz Yisrael.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: Bucharest pogrom kills about one hundred twenty Jews
note: Around 120 Jewish deaths in pogroms in Bucharest.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: Farhud massacre kills Jews in Baghdad
note: Farhud massacre kills Jews in Baghdad.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: Croatian regime confiscates Jewish property and mandates the yellow badge
note: The Axis-aligned Independent State of Croatia confiscated Jewish property and required Jews to wear a yellow identifying badge.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: Nazi Germany invades the Soviet Union
note: Operation Barbarossa opened the vast eastern front. Mobile killing units and their collaborators soon escalated from selective shootings to the murder of entire Jewish communities.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: Mass shootings begin at Ponary near Vilna
note: Mass shootings begin at Ponary near Vilna.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: Nazis kill one thousand Jewish men from Augustów
note: 1,000 Jewish men killed on the day of the German attack on the Soviet Union.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: Sugihara visas enable Jewish refugees and yeshiva students to escape through Japan
note: Polish and Lithuanian Jewish refugees, including yeshiva students, used transit visas associated with Japanese diplomat Chiune Sugihara to travel across the Soviet Union to Japan and later Shanghai.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 286

name: American Vaad Hatzalah rescue work expands under Rabbi Eliezer Silver
note: Rabbi Eliezer Silver and the Agudath Harabonim's Vaad Hatzalah raised large sums and used passports, smugglers and other channels to rescue European Torah scholars and other Jews.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 287

name: R. Elchanan Wasserman is murdered by the Nazis
note: R. Elchanan Wasserman, rosh yeshiva of Baranowicze, among the leading Lithuanian Torah scholars murdered by the Nazis.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 287

name: R. Avraham Yitzchak Bloch and R. Azriel Rabinovitz of Telz are murdered
note: The two Telz roshei yeshiva among the leading Lithuanian scholars killed by the Nazis.
source: Chronological Index of Jewish History, p. 287

name: R. Aharon Kotler escapes via Japan and reaches the United States
note: The Kletsk rosh yeshiva escaped through the Far East and reached the United States, later establishing a major yeshiva in Lakewood.

name: R. Yosef Kahaneman escapes Europe and settles in Eretz Yisrael
